articles.title: Fun things to do with your VM/370 CE machine – Fun with big computers
articles.body:
Fun things to do with your VM/370 CE machine
What can I do with a VM/370 CE mainframe?
This page assumes you have a machine (emulated or not) running the VM370 Community Edition OS available. There are a couple ways to get one, and you might want to choose the one that appeals to you the most (or the one that’s less work - it’s up to you).
What is the Community Edition?
The Community Edition is a huge set of improvements and fixes applied on top of the last VM/370 that was released by IBM without a license restricting its use. These improvements and fixes have been developed and published in a variety of ways since the release of the original OS. If we were to compare it with Linux, VM/370 R6 (the release CE is based on) would be Linux 1.0 as published by Linus from his bedroom and VM/370 CE would be latest Fedora (insert your favorite maximalist distro here). It has many features that didn’t exist in R6 and a couple things that would have been called science fiction back then. It’s quite capable, even if the machines it can run on are limited to a single CPU and 16M of memory (IBM calls it “storage”).
Running with Docker
The easiest way to run this is with Docker installed. How to install it depends on your platform, and we won’t cover it here. Besides, Docker is only one option - you can use Podman as well - it has some nice features, and can pretend it’s Docker, so you can use the same commands with both. When you are set up, you can just issue a shell command to have your own machine.
docker run -it --name vm370 -p 3270:3270 rbanffy/vm370ce
This will bring up the machine and display the machine’s console on your terminal.
The container image we are using is based on the excellent work of the VM/370 Community Edition team. You can see their releases on vm370.org. The Community Editions runs only software that’s either open source or public domain.
Other options for getting a mainframe
If you work in an organization that’s cool enough to have an actual IBM mainframe, you can check if your operations team will allow you to have a small VM running nested VM/370 Community Edition. IBM mainframes have legendary backwards compatibility and there should be no (technical) issue bringing up an environment for you. There might be a lot of process hurdles, however, so tread carefully and have a good excuse at hand. “Doing fun stuff” is not it. Trust me, I’ve tried this approach and it didn’t end well.
Another possible source of used mainframes is eBay or your local IT asset disposal company, but, seriously, you probably don’t want the hassle of a dedicated power line for the machine, or the basement space to have one. And, if you get a real machine, you might also get a valid license to run something more modern, like z/VM, z/OS, and a fairly modern Linux. They are also quite expensive and require expertise to set them up, and, many times, to fix them (people who decommission these machines often don’t bother disconnecting cables when just cutting is faster).
3270 terminals
IBM mainframes use screen-oriented terminals. They worked more or less like a web browser - the mainframe would send you a screen with a form, you’d write some information on the fields of the form, and the terminal would send the information back to the mainframe, restarting the cycle. If you think this looks like how HTML forms work, you are right, but this was in the late 1960s, not the mid 1990s.
Our examples use the x3270 emulator that’s available on any modern Unix-like environment (which includes Linux).
Start x3270 and connect it to your host. If you are running on your computer, it’ll be “localhost:3270”. Since I’m running mine on a small cluster, I’ll point the terminal to the entry address in the cluster.
With that taken out of our way, we can start to have fun.
Logging on
For normal things, we’ll log on to the CMSUSER VM, or, if you renamed it, to your own VM. The default password is “CMSUSER”:
On the banner screen, press ENTER.
The screen will clear. You can then enter logon cmsuser:
And enter the password, “cmsuser”:
As expected, the password isn’t shown. The red cursor means that.
You can also logon using LOGON CMSUSER CMSUSER, typing the password after the user name, but that horrifies me even more than having the username as the password. Back when VM/370 was invented, intrusions were a lot less of a problem than they are now. Please do not expose your VM/370 mainframe directly on the internet.
At this point, you are logged on. There is a lot going on under the hood - CP, or “control program” asked VM/370 to create a virtual machine for you, and this virtual machine was started with the CMS operating system. The commands we’ll see are CMS commands (unless noted). When you press ENTER again, a program, called “PROFILE EXEC” will run:
We can examine it. Note that “PROFILE EXEC” means the name is “PROFILE” and the type is “EXEC” (a script). To show the contents of the file, use:
TYPE PROFILE EXEC
Unlike Unix, commands and file names are case insensitive, so it’s fine to type them either way. Be careful, however, so you don’t overwrite your files accidentally.
Unlike most terminals, a 3270 doesn’t scroll. If you fill the screen, you’ll need to press the PA2 key (don’t look for one on your keyboard - there isn’t one). PA2 clears the terminal and receives the next page of text from the mainframe. On x3270, PA2 is Alt-2. On c3270, it’s Control-C.
Customising your PROFILE EXEC
Our current PROFILE EXEC prints a welcome message that’s informative, but that we can always read later. Let’s remove that message from our profile. For that, we’ll use a little bit of the EDIT editor.
EDIT PROFILE EXEC
Now we need to move down 12 lines. The command space is in the bottom of the screen, with the green cursor. Enter DOWN 12. This will move the highlight to the line we want to delete. Now use the DELETE command.
Now, to save the file and exit, enter FILE. You’ll see the MORE prompt in the bottom right - this indicates you need to press the PA2 key (Alt-2) to continue. 3270 terminals are screen oriented (think web browsers in the 1960s) and don’t scroll - you need to ask them for the next page. This has the advantage of allowing you to edit information on your screen and only causing the computer (the mainframe, in our case) to pay attention when you send it the information you edited. Most other computers that use terminals have to deal with each keystroke separately.
With this change done, the welcome message will not be displayed when you log in. If you want to see it again, you’ll need to type TYPE WELCOME MESSAGE U. Try it.
Running a BASIC program
What is a vintage computer without a BASIC interpreter, right?
Let’s start with the most basic BASIC program: a Hello World.
On your terminal, type:
EDIT HELLO BASIC
Note that “basic” is not a suffix, but a type - it’s a separate parameter. The type of the file is a property of the file and will remain with it unless forcibly changed.
When you press enter (or send) you’ll end up on the EDIT program. On the surface, it looks a lot like vi from the Unix side: it’s terse, hard to use, and sometimes counter-intuitive. It’s also hard to guess how to exit it. That’s about where the similarities end.
Let’s start typing our program:
10 print 'hello world'
When you press enter, you’ll see the line was entered. It was also changed to uppercase (see the “CASE=U” at the top line?). Let’s save the file and quit the editor. Type “file” and press Enter.
The line at the bottom shows a “MORE…” note. This means the terminal is waiting for you before it shows more output. Press PA2 (Alt-2 for x3270) and you’ll see you have exited EDIT.
Now we can run our program:
BASIC HELLO
You’ll see your command (“basic hello”) show up at the top of the screen (after the message indicating EDIT finished), then the message you ordered it to print “HELLO WORLD”, followed by another line telling how much CPU it used and how long did it take to run your program.
A bit of FORTRAN
VM/370 CE comes with a couple hello world programs. You can use the DIR command (which is also something added to vanilla VM) to list what files are in the disk you are seeing. We typed our own in BASIC, but there is one in C and one in FORTRAN. Let’s see the FORTRAN one:
TYPE HELLO FORTRAN
Let’s compile that FORTRAN program (so we can run it)
To compile it, run:
FORTRAN HELLO
The computer will output:
FORTRAN IV (G) COMPILATION COMPLETE.
Ready; T=0.84/2.59 23:39:34
It’s about time we mention the message. It’s telling me the program run using 0.84 seconds of CPU and took 2.59 seconds to complete. It also told me what time it is for the computer.
After compiling the program, you might have noticed two new files appeared:
HELLO    LISTING  A1  F   120     19      3  01/09/26   23:39  CMS191
HELLO    TEXT     A1  F    80     14      2  01/09/26   23:39  CMS191
The first one is a nicely formatted listing, and, in ancient times, you’d find it printed alongside the punched cards you submitted for compilation. It is formatted for 132 columns, as big printers of the time used to be.
   FORTRAN IV G LEVEL  21                 MAIN              DATE = 26009  TIME = 23.39.33             PAGE 0001
    0001              WRITE(6,1)                                                        HEL00010
    0002         1    FORMAT('HELLO WORLD FROM FORTRAN')                                HEL00020
    0003              STOP                                                              HEL00030
    0004              END                                                               HEL00040
   FORTRAN IV G LEVEL  21                 MAIN              DATE = 26009  TIME = 23.39.33             PAGE 0002
                                SUBPROGRAMS CALLED
  SYMBOL    LOCATION      SYMBOL    LOCATION      SYMBOL    LOCATION      SYMBOL    LOCATION      SYMBOL    LOCATION
  IBCOM#        90
                                FORMAT STATEMENT MAP
  SYMBOL    LOCATION      SYMBOL    LOCATION      SYMBOL    LOCATION      SYMBOL    LOCATION      SYMBOL    LOCATION
       1        94
     *OPTIONS IN EFFECT*  ID,EBCDIC,SOURCE,NOLIST,NODECK,LOAD,MAP
     *OPTIONS IN EFFECT*  NAME = MAIN    , LINECNT =       60
     *STATISTICS*    SOURCE STATEMENTS =        4,PROGRAM SIZE =      298
     *STATISTICS*  NO DIAGNOSTICS GENERATED
The other is telling me it’s a text, but it appears it’s a lie:
In order to run the Fortran program we just compiled, we’ll do:
LOAD HELLO ( START
Let’s see what that means:
So… LOAD will load one or more relocatable object code, which is the TEXT file (we knew it was a lie!). So, we are asking LOAD to load the HELLO TEXT file, and we are passing the START option to it (so the code runs).
LOAD HELLO ( START
Execution begins...
Ready; T=1.23/3.90 00:09:54
Looks like nothing happened. But it actually did. There is a new file:
FILE     FT06F001 A1  V    24      1      1  01/10/26    0:09  CMS191
If we look into it, we’ll see:
So, the program ran, and the output went into this oddly named file. This is the first parameter of the WRITE statement. WRITE(6,1) means write to file 6 using the format defined on the line labeled 1. You can also see the “6” in the middle of the file type. We can redirect the output of file 6 to the terminal:
FILEDEF 6 TERMINAL
Now the program outputs to the terminal. Why the first character is missing is an interesting problem. I am not sure why this is happening, neither are my current mainframe gurus. Our current best guess is that this is because the first character of a line being interpreted by the line printer. This is arcane knowledge I don’t fully understand myself, The “right” way to output to a terminal is, and I’ve seen it done in period source code, have a space in the first column of the output string. When the system is outputting to a file, it deals with the output and the first character is suppressed, as it would be by the printer.
What was the magic we used to redirect? Let’s see what FILEDEF does. Do a HELP FILEDEF:
FILEDEF                                                   CMS Transient command
Use the FILEDEF command to establish data definitions for OS ddnames, to define
files to be copied with the MOVEFILE command, or to override default file
definitions made by the assembler and the OS language processors.  The format
of the FILEDEF command is:
+----------+------------------------------------------------------------------+
| FIledef  | ddname nn *  device                                              |
|          |                                                                  |
|          | device:                                                          |
|          |    Terminal [(optionA optionD[)]]                                |
|          |    PRinter  [(optionD[)]]                                        |
|          |    PUnch    [(optionD[)]]                                        |
|          |    Reader   [(optionD[)]]                                        |
|          |    DISK [FILE|fn ddname|ft [A1|fm]] [DSN ?|q1 q2 ...]            |
|          |             [(optionA optionB[)]]                                |
|          |    DUMMY    [(optionA[)]]                                        |
|          |    TAPn     [(optionA optionC[)]]                                |
|          |    CLEAR                                                         |
|          | optionA:                                                         |
|          |    BLOCK|BLKSIZE nnnnn  CHANGE|NOCHANGE     LRECL nnnnn          |
|          |    PERM                 RECFM a                                  |
|          | optionB:                                                         |
|          |    CONCAT               DISP MOD            DSORG PS|PO|DA|IS    |
|          |    KEYLEN nnn           LIMCT nnn           MEMBER name          |
|          |    OPTCD a              XTENT 50|nnnnn                           |
|          | optionC:                                                         |
|          |    7TRACK|9TRACK        TRTCH a             DEN den              |
|          | optionD:                                                         |
|          |    UPCASE|LOWCASE                                                |
+----------+------------------------------------------------------------------+
where:
ddname | nn | *
         is the name  by which the file is referred to in your program.  OS
         ddname syntax rules should be followed.  If a number nn is specified,
         it is translated to a FORTRAN data definition name of FTnnF001.  An
         asterisk (*) may be specified with the CLEAR operand to indicate that
         all file definitions not entered with the PERM option should be
         cleared.
Devices:
Terminal is your terminal (terminal I/O must not be blocked).  Terminal input
         will be truncated to the console input buffer length of 130
         characters.
… and so on. Fortran, by default, outputs to whatever is defined as file “6”, which ends up being “FILE FT06F001”. This is all related to the way batch processes were set up where things like input and outputs were specified by a configuration for when a program is run. This was done in a language called JCL (for Job Control Language). It was uncommon for programs to be run interactively at the terminal, and even having a terminal was considered a luxury most programmers didn’t have - they’d submit their code in special forms that someone else would type, convert to punch cards, and feed to the compiler.
Running our own programs
There is a lot of code you can use. For exaple, the IBM System/360 Operating System FORTRAN IV Programmer’s Guide has an example, primes.fortran I copied into this repo:
C PRIME NUMBER PROBLEM
C FROM IBM System/360 Operating System FORTRAN IV Programmers Guide
C https://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/360/fortran/
C GC28-6817-4_OS360_FORTRAN_IV_G_and_H_Programmers_Guide_197309.pdf
C page 108
C Modified for brevity from 1 to 1000 to 1 to 100
  100 WRITE (6,8)
    8 FORMAT (52H FOLLOWING IS A LIST OF PRIME NUMBERS FROM 1 TO 100 /
     X 119X,1H1/19X,1H2/19X,1H3)
  101 I=5
    3 A=I
  102 A=SQRT(A)
  103 J=A
  104 DO 1 K=3,J,2
  105 L=I/K
  106 IF(L*K-I)1,2,4
    1 CONTINUE
  107 WRITE (6,5)I
    5 FORMAT (I20)
    2 I=I+2
  108 IF(100-I)7,4,3
    4 WRITE (6,9)
    9 FORMAT (14H PROGRAM ERROR)
    7 WRITE (6,6)
    6 FORMAT (31H THIS IS THE END OF THE PROGRAM)
  109 STOP
      END
When you upload it, make sure it’s fixed length at 80 characters, as punched cards were. If you forget, you’ll get a helpful error message:
FILE 'PRIMES FORTRAN' IS NOT FIXED, 80 CHAR. RECORDS.
Upload like this:
You’ll now see that the file is now of fixed 80 character width (F 80 in the format column).
Filename Filetype Fm  Format    Recs Blocks    Date     Time   Label
...
PRIMES   FORTRAN  A1  F    80     27      3  01/11/26   14:47  CMS191
Now you can compile and run it:
Again we see some oddness at the start of the output.
… but we can see the program completed successfully.
Other interesting languages available
PL/I
PL/I is another language popular in mainframes, and is used to this day. It’s much closer to more to what users of other recent languages would find familiar. It even includes a C-like preprocessor that allows including external files, conditional compilation and code-generating loops.
To invoke the compiler, use:
PLI FILENAME1 [FILENAME2 ... FILENAMEn]
This will compile all the files mentioned. The compiler has lots of options, so it’s a good idea to read the built-in for the compiler. For that, as usual, type:
HELP PLI
REXX
Rexx is the “glue language” of IBM mainframes. It’s simple, easy to use and interpreted. To write a REXX program you use the text editor. Using the file type EXEC will make it callable from the command line, but, in order for it to be recognized as a REXX program, the first line needs to be a comment delimited by /* and */. The language itself reminds me of later versions of BASIC after line numbers were no longer a thing:
/* REXX program to display the first 20 prime numbers */
count = 0
num = 2
DO WHILE count < 20
  IF is_prime(num) THEN DO
    SAY num
    count = count + 1
  END
  num = num + 1
END
EXIT
is_prime: PROCEDURE
  ARG n
  IF n < 2 THEN
    RETURN 0
  DO divisor = 2 TO TRUNC(SQRT(n))
    IF n // divisor = 0 THEN
      RETURN 0
  END
  RETURN 1
C
Pascal
ALGOL
This is interesting - there is a VM without a login that has the name ALGOL. [TBA]
Navigating the disks
The VM370CE distribution has a lot of disks. You can check which ones you have immediate access with. If you logged on as CMSUSER, you can use the LISTFILE (we abreviated it to “LIST”) command to see what files are on your default disk. In CMS, commands can be abbreviated - the actual command is LISTFILE but LIST is neat enough.
To check the disks you have, use QUERY DISK (query can also be abbreviated - Q will suffice for the computer to understand what you want):
To list what’s on a disk, you’ll use LISTFILE * * [disk]. The first “*” is a wildcard that will show all file names, the second is for all types. If you are familiar with windcards from CP/M, MS-DOS, or Unix, these don’t behave the same.
The third parameter is the disk:
So… Looking at the output of LISTFILE and LISTFILE * * A, we can conclude we were start from disk A. In this case, A is a shortcut to disk 191 (mainframes always were supposed to have lots of disks, and our emulated one - a maxed out 4381 - has more than most companies could afford, or that would fit in most period accurate computer rooms). In our case, 191 is the “address” of the disk, and tells where the disk is connected to the virtual machine. Disks also have 6-character labels (or “VOLSER” in mainframe slang). A is “CMS190”.
Let’s check the other disks:
Disks D, E, F, and G are empty. That wouldn’t be a surprise if we had paid attention to the output of QUERY DISK - it clearly says they have zero files, and use 5 blocks (rounded to 0% of the disk).
There is also disk S (or 190, or ). It has 172 files, so it’ll take a couple pages to list everything. In the list you’ll see a lot of interesting files - this disk contains system utilities - there’s ACCESS, EDIT, QUERY, SET, SORT, GLOBAL, and other things that we have seen before or that look like things an OS would provide (not a big surprise, as its label is “CMSDSK”). Binary programs seem to be of type “MODULE”. Let’s remember that. Try listing all files of type MODULE in S:
DIR * MODULE S
CMS offers a flat file system, so we can’t have subdirectories. This is a big difference for people who are used to Unix or Windows systems and to organize files using them. Another difference, that’ll feel more familiar to Windows users (and CP/M users before them) is that the system exposes multiple volumes instead of the single-root hierarchy of Unix systens.
Finally, a more subtle difference is that there is no such thing as the “current” disk. If you don’t specify a disk letter, the file is interpreted as A, which is your “home”. You don’t ever “change” to another disk, and you always mention them explicitly.
A plain VM/370 would map CMS system files to disk S. The Community Edition we are running has the OS on drive S, and OS extras on disk Y. Disk U contains utilities.
Uploading files to your machine (and playing games)
For this example, we’ll use the GAMES.VMARC file available at the h390-vm group at groups.io. The easiest way to upload a file to your mainframe is with the x3270 app - on the File menu select “File Transfer”:
Since we are uploading a VMARC file (think a .zip or .tar.bz2), we’ll chose a binary transfer. The file will be saved to our disk D.
It might be a while if you are running Hercules on an underpowered Raspberry Pi Zero W. I assume a local instance on a sensible computer will be a lot faster. When the transfer is finished, a new dialog will pop up telling you so.
Now we need to understand how to open a VMARC file. Luckily for us, VM370CE has a very comprehensive help system. On the terminal, issue a:
HELP VMARC
Listing the contents of the file seems like a good first step:
VMARC LIST GAMES VMARC D
Let’s get one of the games:
VMARC UNPACK GAMES VMARC D TICTOE MODULE D
It’s there!
Now we want to run it.
TICTOE
… and it works!
As most people know, the only winning move with Tic Tac Toe (and Global Thermonuclear War) is not to play. The other games are a lot more interesting.
Moar games
Other two game archives that are easy to obtain are under the VM-370-Games repo on Github. Once you download the files to your desktop and sent them to your VM/370 machine, you’ll have:
Filename Filetype Fm  Format    Recs Blocks    Date     Time   Label
VM86F155 VMARC    D1  V    80  15578   1597  01/03/26    1:20  CMS192
ZORK     VMARC    D1  V    80   8865    909  01/03/26    0:37  CMS192
The first one, VM86F155, has a lot of games in BASIC you can explore and modify (it you figure out how EDIT works).
The ZORK code is in FORTRAN, and, while there is a program called GENZORK, it fails (maybe it needs to run on a disk at B).
Let me know if you figure it out.
[Solution TBA]
We are done with CMSUSER for now, so we’ll be good users and log off our machine:
Adding a user for you
It’s no fun to log in as CMSUSER every time you want to do something. You’ll want a user for yourself, with reasonable permissions to do things to the machine. In my case, I want to create an “RBANFFY” user for me.
Here’s the first surprise for those who come from other platforms - you wouldn’t create a user, you’d create a VM, and you log in to that VM. You can create a user without creating a VM for it, but that would not be what you actually want. Users and VMs are defined the same way, with the USER keyword.
Creating a VM is a bit involved - you’ll need to do a lot of things before - allocate and format storage, for instance. We’ll leave that for later.
In the meantime, if you want to rename the CMSUSER VM to your preferred name (and change the password), we can explain that. We’ll start logging on as MAINT (which means, logging on to the MAINT VM).
We’ll also learn a lot of interesting things about our system, and a couple new commands for the EDIT editor.
Editing USER DIRECT
The first thing we want to do is to check which disks are available to this VM.
Note that we share a couple disks with other VMs. This is counterintuitive to people used to do VMs the Windows or Linux way - under VM/370 (and its descendants) VMs can share filesystems, not disks. Think of it as mounting a remote filesystem, but there is no remote server - this is done within the hypervisor. We are sharing volumes CMSDSK, MNT29D and MNT19E with other users (we saw it logged in as CMSUSER).
The file we want to look into is USER DIRECT. Let’s first find where it is located. Use LISTFILE USER DIRECT * to list files named USER DIRECT in all volumes you can access. Your terminal will show something like:
LISTFILE USER DIRECT *
USER     DIRECT   A1
Ready; T=0.07/0.13 12:20:46
So, we see the file is in our default disk (A), which is volume MNT191. Let’s edit it - on your terminal, run EDIT USER DIRECT.
The top line tells you the file and the mode you are working in.
EDIT    USER     DIRECT   A1  F  80 ZONE=  1- 72 VERFY=  1- 72 CASE=U TRUNC= 72
This tells me we have the USER DIRECT file, located on A (ignore the 1 for now), that it is a fixed line length file of 80 columns (F  80), and that everything we type will be converted to uppercase (CASE=U). It also says TRUNC= 72 to tell us we can’t go past column 72. This was used for punchcards to identify the card (which is a line in the file).
To navigate, you can use EDIT’s commands up and down. When you follow them with a number, they repeat the operation that number of times. If you are lost, you can use top or bottom to get to the top of the end of the bottom of the file. Let’s do a DOWN 14.
This is how you define VMs. They are called users here, so you might be confused. Some VMs start automatically while others will only be started on LOGON (and will shut down on LOGOFF). This first definitions are, as the comment explains, created to make it easier to define your own users, and you can’t log-on to them yourself.
The file gets more interesting when you look at the ASSIST user. Do a LOCATE ASSIST:
  Note: The user ALGOL is also interesting, but we won’t talk about it right now.
Here you see a couple commands before the disk definitions. They tell the user will log-on to the CMS operating environment (IPL means “Initial Program Load” and is what other systems would call “boot”). It’ll then tell how the console is to be used (like an IBM 3215 console as device 009). It’ll also set up a card reader/puncher (one IBM 2540 connected on 00C and 00D) and a printer (an IBM 1403).
USER ASSIST ASSIST 15M 16M G
 IPL CMS
 CONSOLE 009 3215
 SPOOL 00C 2540 READ A
 SPOOL 00D 2540 PUNCH A
 SPOOL 00E 1403 A
  Note: The first line tells us the user name (ASSISS), the password (yes, in clear text), and how much memory the machine should have allocated.
Let’s now look into the user we might want to rename. In EDIT, do a LOCATE CMSUSER:
USER CMSUSER CMSUSER 15M 16M G
 IPL CMS
 CONSOLE 009 3215
 SPOOL 00E 1403 A
 SPOOL 00C 2540 READ *
 SPOOL 00D 2540 PUNCH A
 LINK MAINT 190 190 RR
 LINK MAINT 19D 19D RR
 LINK MAINT 19E 19E RR
*        cuu type adr num volser mode readpw   writepw  multpw
 MDISK   191 3350 001 115 VM50U0 MR   ALL      WRITE    MULT
 MDISK   192 3350 116 115 VM50U0 MR   ALL      WRITE    MULT
 MDISK   193 3350 231 115 VM50U0 MR   ALL      WRITE    MULT
 MDISK   194 3350 346 115 VM50U0 MR   ALL      WRITE    MULT
 MDISK   195 3350 461 094 VM50U0 MR   ALL      WRITE    MULT
Now you’ll want to open a second x3270 window and log on as CMSUSER.
LOGON CMSUSER CMSUSER
DASD 190 LINKED R/O; R/W BY MAINT; R/O BY 004 USERS
DASD 19D LINKED R/O; R/W BY MAINT; R/O BY 002 USERS
DASD 19E LINKED R/O; R/W BY MAINT; R/O BY 004 USERS
LOGON AT 13:10:22 GMT MONDAY 01/19/26
VM Community Edition V1 R1.2
Notice these are the 3 disks mentioned in the LINK commands after the card reader/puncher and the printer are added. They are being linked from the user MAINT
When there, do a QUERY DISK:
 Label  CUU M  Stat  Cyl Type Blksize   Files  Blks Used-(%) Blks Left  Blk Total
CMS191 191 A   R/W  115 3350  800          7        111-00      65420      65531
CMS192 192 D   R/W  115 3350  800          0          5-00      65526      65531
CMS193 193 E   R/W  115 3350  800          0          5-00      65526      65531
CMS194 194 F   R/W  115 3350  800          0          5-00      65526      65531
CMS195 195 G   R/W   94 3350  800          0          5-00      53575      53580
CMSDSK 190 S   R/O   59 3350  800        172      19537-58      14093      33630
MNT29D 19D U/S R/O   30 3350  800        407       6242-37      10858      17100
MNT19E 19E Y/S R/O   70 3350  800        710      28263-71      11637      39900
Ready; T=0.13/0.82 13:19:36
The first five disks are the ones defined in USER DIRECT in the MDISK lines. The last 3 are the ones LINK’ed from MAIN.
To exit EDIT saving your changes, use the FILE command. To leave without saving changes, use QUIT. You’ll need to clear the terminal to continue (the “MORE…” message in the bottom right). On x3270 PA2, which clears the terminal, is Alt-2.
Another interesting file you might look into. It is a comprehensive list of all disk partitioins, the users those partitions are used by, the CUU they are attached to, and the start and end of the partition, in cylinders. All entries look like this one:
VOLUME   USERID      CUU   DEVTYPE   START      END     SIZE
GCCBRX   $ALLOC$     110      3350   00000    00000    00001
                                     00001    00050    00050    GAP
         MAINTC      293      3350   00051    00100    00050
         MAINTC      191      3350   00101    00150    00050
         MAINTC      394      3350   00151    00200    00050
         MAINTC      194      3350   00201    00250    00050
         MAINTC      395      3350   00251    00300    00050
         MAINTC      393      3350   00301    00350    00050
         MAINTC      193      3350   00351    00400    00050
         MAINTC      493      3350   00401    00450    00050
         MAINTC      19C      3350   00451    00500    00050
         MAINTC      195      3350   00501    00550    00050
         MAINTC      295      3350   00551    00551    00001
Creating a new user (or VM) would be more work than I’d like to cover here. It’d mean adding new disks, partitioning them, creating filesystems, and adding them to the configuration. Perhaps more importantly, it’d require me to learn a whole lot of things before I could confidently do it.
So, instead of creating a new user, we’ll change the CMSUSER user name and password (passwords can’t have more than 8 characters and are case insensitive). Keep in mind this is how it used to be in the 1970s - modern mainframes are much better protected.
My plan of having a user for me, one for my wife, and users for my kids will have to wait for another day.
Updating the USER directory
[TBA]
Viewing files without using TYPE
TYPE is a fine command (those with CP/M and MS-DOS experience will remember it), but VM/370 CE bundles a full-screen file viewer.
[TBA]
Using other text editors
So far we have used EDIT. It’s an editor that comes with IBM’s VM/370 R6 and is the one you might see in period videos, but we have another one that’s much nicer: EE.
On your termminal, write:
EE PROFILE EXEC
Using EE
Typing EE PROFILE EXEC brings up the editor, in our case, with the PROFILE EXEC file loaded.
EE is a much modern editor, and behaves like current tools, such as ISPF. One nice thing it has is the command are on the left (that region filled with equals signs). Move the cursor up and enter “i3” on one.
When you hit enter, you’ll see EE inserted 3 lines (because that’s what i and 3 mean in this context).
To enter new text (or change what’s on the screen), just move the cursor there and start typing.
We really don’t want that sitting in our PROFILE EXEC file, so we’ll remove those 3 lines.
Now the file is the same as when we started. Pay attention to the purple line at the bottom, and press F3 to quit EE.
Tricked you! F3 will not work because we changed the file (EE doesn’t realize the contents are the same as they are on disk). We’ll use the QQuit command to quit. Think of it as “:q!” on Vim.
Talking to other mainframes
Mounting a disk on another running Hercules instance
Hercules can run without a UI in Shared Device Server mode. In this mode, it can start and no environment needs to be IPL’ed.
[Details TBA]
TCP/IP networking on VM370
[TBA]
Printing
To a virtual printer
Hercules supports routing a printer to a local file. On the packaged version of MVT 3.8j a 1403 line printer is mapped to the prt/prt00f.txt file, and on VM/370 there are two 1403 printers, mapped to io/print1.listing and io/print2.listing. On the container images, these files are not exposed to the host directly, and you’ll have to map the container folder to the host yourself.
To a real printer
[TBA]
Using a “normal” terminal
Enabling access via a printing terminal (not screen-based).
Where to get more software
https://www.vm.ibm.com/download/packages/# https://vmworkshop.org/HENSLER/
Other resources
https://www.leeandmelindavarian.com/Melinda/

articles.title: Payments Canada announces launch of Canada's Real-Time Rail (RTR) payment system
articles.body:
Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy
The new system will enable participating financial service providers to clear and settle payments in real time, providing a made-in-Canada platform for future innovation and prosperity.
OTTAWA, ON, November 9, 2026 – Payments Canada today announced the launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR). This new national payment system will transform day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers by enabling instant speed and settlement, real-time cash-flow visibility and data-rich messaging through existing banking and payment channels.
The launch of Canada’s RTR marks a major milestone in modernizing the critical infrastructure that underpins Canada’s economy and future growth. The RTR will enable participating members, including financial institutions, credit unions and payment service providers, to exchange, clear and settle payments securely in real time for their customers, 24 hours a day, every day of the year.
“A stronger, more productive economy relies on modern financial infrastructure that can match our ambition,” said the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail lays the foundation for a more dynamic and competitive digital economy, driving innovation, expanding choice and creating new opportunities for Canadians while positioning our country for long-term growth.”
“The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail marks the beginning of a new era for payments in our country,” said Susan E. Hawkins, President and CEO, Payments Canada. “As a national asset that’s designed specifically for our country, the RTR gives the payment ecosystem a modern foundation to build on. By collectively leveraging this rail, our ecosystem will unleash its full potential, enabling our members to build capabilities that drive innovation, resilience and growth for businesses and consumers across the nation.”
Ron Morrow, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne and Susan E. Hawkins
The RTR will drive significant cost savings and economic growth in Canada over the next decade. The C.D. Howe Institute projects that, with its functionalities at launch, the RTR will generate up to $14.5 billion in cost savings from lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques, and reduced float (the period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient). Extending beyond these cost savings, the RTR is expected to generate $16 billion in economic gains, growing to $27 billion as new functionalities are introduced over time.
“The Real-Time Rail is an important step in modernizing Canada's payment infrastructure and ensuring it keeps pace with Canadians' evolving needs,” said Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. “The Bank will oversee the system so that it operates safely and reliably while ensuring Canadians can benefit from innovations in financial services.”
Owned and operated by Payments Canada, and built in collaboration with delivery partners CGI, Deloitte Canada, IBM Canada and Interac Corp., the RTR leverages ISO 20022 data-rich messaging. Through this shared technical language, the RTR holds the potential to strengthen Canada’s economic sovereign autonomy and support its global competitiveness.
Fraud safeguards from day one
Canada is the first G7 country to deploy a real-time payment system with mandatory centralized fraud services for use at launch. These services will be used alongside participants’ existing fraud controls to mitigate the risk of fraud for Canadian businesses and consumers at multiple levels. Fraud controls required at the launch of Canada’s RTR include:
- Confirmation of payee (available for consumer accounts on day one)
- A fraud transaction “safety” score
- A risk list or repository of fraud risks and indicators
- A fraud reporting and intelligence platform
While no system is entirely immune to risk, these measures establish a strong, coordinated layer of defence across the payment network.
At-launch member participants
The initial cohort of active RTR system participants includes:
- Wealthsimple
- Questbank
- Peoples Trust Company
- Paramount Commerce
- KOHO
- DoBusiness.com™
- Digital Commerce Bank
- Bank of America
Canada’s deliberately sequenced RTR rollout pairs day-one security with rapid scalability. With additional participants onboarding continually in the coming months, including all major Canadian financial institutions and other members applying for access, the RTR will be available to more than nine in 10 Canadians within the first year after launch.
Made-in Canada, for Canada
The launch of the RTR reflects our ‘Team Canada’ approach, bringing together regulators, members, stakeholders and delivery partners around a shared vision. Built in Canada and designed to serve all Canadians, the RTR provides accessible payment infrastructure through existing banking and payment channels. This infrastructure supports a diverse country and a broad range of communities, including small businesses, newcomers and people in rural areas.
Payments Canada research found that 60 per cent of Canadian businesses are ready to adopt real-time payments to address everyday challenges such as forecasting cash flow and waiting to send and receive funds. More than half of surveyed consumers (52 per cent) also expressed interest and intent to use real-time payments.
To meet this evolving need, the RTR serves as a secure platform for innovation. With it, system participants can build and offer products and services that benefit consumers and businesses across the country, supporting a changing economy and Canada's future prosperity.
An infrastructure for the future
Canada’s Real-Time Rail is an important step toward a more productive, innovative and inclusive economy, and the work will continue to ensure the country’s payment infrastructure meets Canadians’ evolving needs.
Learn more about Canada’s Real-Time Rail
Contributed quotes
At-launch member participants
"When Canada embraces new technology, innovation and competition follow, and consumers benefit. Canadians deserve instant, seamless, low-cost financial products to power their businesses and their lives. The Real-Time Rail can transform how money moves in this country, with payments that arrive in seconds instead of days. We’re proud to be among the first institutions to join the RTR and bring this technology to the millions of Canadians who trust us with their money."
Mike Katchen, CEO and Co-Founder

articles.title: Payments Canada announces launch of Canada's Real-Time Rail (RTR) payment system
articles.body:
Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy
The new system will enable participating financial service providers to clear and settle payments in real time, providing a made-in-Canada platform for future innovation and prosperity.
OTTAWA, ON, November 9, 2026 – Payments Canada today announced the launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR). This new national payment system will transform day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers by enabling instant speed and settlement, real-time cash-flow visibility and data-rich messaging through existing banking and payment channels.
The launch of Canada’s RTR marks a major milestone in modernizing the critical infrastructure that underpins Canada’s economy and future growth. The RTR will enable participating members, including financial institutions, credit unions and payment service providers, to exchange, clear and settle payments securely in real time for their customers, 24 hours a day, every day of the year.
“A stronger, more productive economy relies on modern financial infrastructure that can match our ambition,” said the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail lays the foundation for a more dynamic and competitive digital economy, driving innovation, expanding choice and creating new opportunities for Canadians while positioning our country for long-term growth.”
“The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail marks the beginning of a new era for payments in our country,” said Susan E. Hawkins, President and CEO, Payments Canada. “As a national asset that’s designed specifically for our country, the RTR gives the payment ecosystem a modern foundation to build on. By collectively leveraging this rail, our ecosystem will unleash its full potential, enabling our members to build capabilities that drive innovation, resilience and growth for businesses and consumers across the nation.”
Ron Morrow, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne and Susan E. Hawkins
The RTR will drive significant cost savings and economic growth in Canada over the next decade. The C.D. Howe Institute projects that, with its functionalities at launch, the RTR will generate up to $14.5 billion in cost savings from lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques, and reduced float (the period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient). Extending beyond these cost savings, the RTR is expected to generate $16 billion in economic gains, growing to $27 billion as new functionalities are introduced over time.
“The Real-Time Rail is an important step in modernizing Canada's payment infrastructure and ensuring it keeps pace with Canadians' evolving needs,” said Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. “The Bank will oversee the system so that it operates safely and reliably while ensuring Canadians can benefit from innovations in financial services.”
Owned and operated by Payments Canada, and built in collaboration with delivery partners CGI, Deloitte Canada, IBM Canada and Interac Corp., the RTR leverages ISO 20022 data-rich messaging. Through this shared technical language, the RTR holds the potential to strengthen Canada’s economic sovereign autonomy and support its global competitiveness.
Fraud safeguards from day one
Canada is the first G7 country to deploy a real-time payment system with mandatory centralized fraud services for use at launch. These services will be used alongside participants’ existing fraud controls to mitigate the risk of fraud for Canadian businesses and consumers at multiple levels. Fraud controls required at the launch of Canada’s RTR include:
- Confirmation of payee (available for consumer accounts on day one)
- A fraud transaction “safety” score
- A risk list or repository of fraud risks and indicators
- A fraud reporting and intelligence platform
While no system is entirely immune to risk, these measures establish a strong, coordinated layer of defence across the payment network.
At-launch member participants
The initial cohort of active RTR system participants includes:
- Wealthsimple
- Questbank
- Peoples Trust Company
- Paramount Commerce
- KOHO
- DoBusiness.com™
- Digital Commerce Bank
- Bank of America
Canada’s deliberately sequenced RTR rollout pairs day-one security with rapid scalability. With additional participants onboarding continually in the coming months, including all major Canadian financial institutions and other members applying for access, the RTR will be available to more than nine in 10 Canadians within the first year after launch.
Made-in Canada, for Canada
The launch of the RTR reflects our ‘Team Canada’ approach, bringing together regulators, members, stakeholders and delivery partners around a shared vision. Built in Canada and designed to serve all Canadians, the RTR provides accessible payment infrastructure through existing banking and payment channels. This infrastructure supports a diverse country and a broad range of communities, including small businesses, newcomers and people in rural areas.
Payments Canada research found that 60 per cent of Canadian businesses are ready to adopt real-time payments to address everyday challenges such as forecasting cash flow and waiting to send and receive funds. More than half of surveyed consumers (52 per cent) also expressed interest and intent to use real-time payments.
To meet this evolving need, the RTR serves as a secure platform for innovation. With it, system participants can build and offer products and services that benefit consumers and businesses across the country, supporting a changing economy and Canada's future prosperity.
An infrastructure for the future
Canada’s Real-Time Rail is an important step toward a more productive, innovative and inclusive economy, and the work will continue to ensure the country’s payment infrastructure meets Canadians’ evolving needs.
Learn more about Canada’s Real-Time Rail

articles.title: Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang
articles.body:
President Trump held a White House press briefing earlier today and responded to several questions about his knowledge of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang said this weekend that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, and the company has opened an investigation into Huang.
Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang
In a White House press conference, President Trump was vague about when learned of Jensen Huang’s affair.
Recent articles from The New York Times indicated that Trump had been aware of a relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, the suspected spy, before information about it became public. In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information. Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May.
In the press conference, Trump wasn’t specific about when he learned of the affair. But Trump said Huang told him today that he had “no idea” the person was a spy.
Here are Trump’s responses to questions about Jensen Huang from his press briefing today. You can watch a replay of the press conference on MS Now’s YouTube channel.
When were you first informed that there was an issue with Jensen Huang and the affair? What was presented to you at the time?
I would say that when I heard about it, first of all, I was amazed because I view him as a very high-quality person. I’ve known him a long time. It’s the largest, by value, the largest or one of the largest companies in the world. He did that with a chip. When you think about it, you’ve got a chip that’s 10 years advanced, can’t be… the Blackwell can’t even be copied. He’s an amazing guy.
I just hope there’s no problem. If there is a problem, we’ll let you know about it. But I hope there’s no problem. I believe he’s suffering greatly. I read his statement. And I believe he’s suffering greatly. Moreso because of his family. His wife who he loves and his family. But he is definitely suffering.
Just to follow up on the, “When were you first told of these potential issues with Mr. Huang?” You didn’t answer that question.
Well I’ve been hearing about it, and I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago.
When is that?
We’ll look into it. I know the FBI’s looking into it in terms of something else. I think that he’ll be in good shape.
…
Are you going to bring up the case of Jensen Huang with President Xi when you visit with him next week?
No, I don’t think so. Maybe, I’m sure, President Xi will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable man. He built a great company. American company. I think he’s a very honorable guy. I feel very confident that he’ll be in good shape.
Sticking with Jensen Huang, when you went to China earlier this year in May, did you know about these alleged ties to the spy then?
No, I didn’t hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it. And Jensen totally denies that. I asked him today, because I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling alright, how are you doing… and I asked him about that. He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy. I asked him that question, did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said, I had no idea that she was a spy. And I really believe him.
…
I want to put a finer point on when exactly you were made aware of the intelligence around Jensen Huang.
Oh, I’d have to check. But this has been going on…
But there are reports that Secretary Rubio put an intelligence memo out last year. Did you read that memo?
I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. It could have been mentioned. Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.

articles.title: Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang
articles.body:
The leather-jacketed CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, has acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, spurring an investigation by his company and intense discussions worldwide. Recent reporting noted that since last year, US intelligence reports had identified Alice Huang (no relation) as not only the exec for an AI compute company renting access to Nvidia GPUs, but also a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.
In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies, including the “neoclouds” like Coreweave who have been some of its biggest customers. So far, Nvidia and Jensen Huang have said that they have “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that hasn’t settled things as the investigation continues.
- What could China get from Jensen Huang? It’s difficult to overstate Nvidia’s power in today’s AI landscape. The company’s chips are the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built, and demand has consistently outpaced supply for years. Nvidia has also been an influential investor in a wide range of up-and-coming AI companies in recent years, with about $99 billion worth of equity investments in frontier AI labs, neoclouds, infrastructure companies, and more. Its chief executive has even become close with President Donald Trump. This is why, as both cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry. Read Article >
- Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang President Trump held a White House press briefing earlier today and responded to several questions about his knowledge of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang said this weekend that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, and the company has opened an investigation into Huang. Recent articles from The New York Times indicated that Trump had been aware of a relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, the suspected spy, before information about it became public. In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information. Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May. Read Article >
- The future of AI hinges on… Jensen Huang’s sex life? I would prefer that these people’s sex lives were none of my business but I guess we have to talk about Jensen Huang and the National Security Incident. Who could have guessed that the guy who was out here signing titties might not have great judgment about how to behave around women? Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — is a former TV reporter. That was before she became “an executive” at Megaspeed, which bought $4.8 billion of hard-to-get Nvidia chips, starting around the time she was being photographed with Jensen in a Taipei bar in 2024. “To many in the industry, the well-funded push by Megaspeed into A.I. appeared to come out of nowhere,” The New York Times wrote, tactfully. Our girl Alice is also an alleged honeypot who was recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security. (China is denying all this, btw.) Read Article >
- Here’s the full text of Jensen Huang’s memo to Nvidia On Sunday, Nvidia announced it was launching an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, an AI executive and agent of the Chinese government. In addition to the Board of Directors announcing the investigation, Huang sent a memo to Nvidia employees acknowledging the affair. You can read the full text below. Read Article >
- Nvidia is investigating Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy Nvidia has announced that it is opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who was reportedly recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on the company. The New York Times reported last month that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with the Megaspeed executive, which he later admitted was romantic in nature in a memo to the company. US officials believe she was feeding information directly back to Beijing. Read Article >

articles.title: Commerce Dept. Chip Inquiry Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention
articles.body:
Commerce Dept. Chip Inquiry Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention (nytimes.com) 39
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: Investigators at the Commerce Department were deep into a monthslong investigation of a Singaporean company that they suspected of smuggling Nvidia's artificial intelligence chips into China when their work came to a sudden halt late last year. The investigation centered on Megaspeed, a data center company led by an executive who U.S. officials now believe to be a Chinese spy who had a relationship with Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang. But the case was abruptly transferred to the Justice Department last year. The shift came after Commerce Department investigators working on the case received an email from Nvidia's general counsel seeking information about the inquiry into Megaspeed.
It is not necessarily unusual for Commerce Department agents working on a case to speak with a company's representatives about issues involving their firm. But what was unusual was the content of the message. Tim Teter, Nvidia's general counsel, said that Jeff Kessler, a top official at the department, had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case. The agents were alarmed that Nvidia had invoked the name of Mr. Kessler, their superior, who was nominated to his role by President Trump. Some viewed Mr. Kessler's interaction with Nvidia as violating government procedure and potentially tainting the case, according to current and former government officials and others familiar with the incident.
It is not clear what led to Mr. Teter's outreach to the department, but the recent revelations about Mr. Huang's acknowledged affair with a Megaspeed executive have only intensified scrutiny of Nvidia's role in influencing policy on chip sales to China. [...] The incident raised questions about what Mr. Kessler, who reports directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, had discussed with Nvidia. It also raised the possibility that those discussions could become their own subject of inquiry. Perhaps inadvertently, some officials said, Mr. Kessler had opened himself to accusations of undue influence and potentially jeopardized his department's work on Megaspeed. The case was quickly transferred to the Justice Department in an effort to avoid any potential compromise of the government's investigation of Megaspeed, these people said. The Justice Department is conducting a criminal inquiry into Megaspeed, according to people familiar with the matter.

articles.title: The race is on to sue Nvidia
articles.body:
Nvidia’s stock slid more than 4% on Monday, the first trading day after its board said it would investigate CEO Jensen Huang over his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive U.S. intelligence believes was spying for China.
Securities lawyers were already moving. At least four firms, including Schall, Brown & Schwartz and Levi & Korsinsky, announced investigations Monday into whether Nvidia misled investors. Robert Bartlett, a Stanford Law professor and securities law expert, expects them to have plenty of company.
“I would definitely wager that there’ll be a filing,” Bartlett said in an interview Monday morning, adding that he wouldn’t be surprised if a case had been filed by the end of the day. Plaintiffs’ lawyers have good reasons to be first in line; under federal securities law, the first complaint triggers a public notice, and investors then have 60 days to ask the court to be named lead plaintiff. A firm that files early gets a head start on signing up investors with large losses, as well as on shaping the story of the case. Bartlett was right, in fact. A case surfaced Monday afternoon in the Northern District of California, where Nvidia is headquartered.
Rosen Law Firm, a New York-based plaintiffs’ firm that specializes in securities class actions, filed it on behalf of Mark Kistenmacher, a retail investor who made seven purchases totaling roughly $20,500 this year, according to a schedule attached to the complaint. (Rosen was lead counsel in a $250 million settlement with Alibaba and ranks among the most active filers of such cases.) The proposed class covers anyone who bought Nvidia securities between Oct. 9, 2025, and Nov. 8, 2026, and the suit names both Nvidia and Huang.
The complaint accuses them of misleading investors about Huang’s ties to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center outfit where Alice Huang was considered a top exec, and it points to three statements as proof: Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo’s late-October claim that Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected,” the company’s even earlier claim that it found “no evidence of diversion” of its chips, and Jensen Huang’s Oct. 30 comment to Bloomberg that Nvidia’s dealings with Megaspeed were “normal and not unusual.”
All three were false or misleading, the suit says, because Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang. Kistenmacher is asking for unspecified damages, interest and attorneys’ fees, and he wants a jury trial.
While much remains unknown, the legal theory here doesn’t depend on anything the board’s investigation may turn up about Huang’s private life. When The New York Times first reported on Huang’s ties to Alice Huang last month, Rizzo really did tell the Times that the relationship was “not unusual or unexpected.” Rizzo separately told another outlet, The Hill, that “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”
Of course, the world now knows that was not true. Worse, the Times reports that U.S. intelligence had been monitoring Alice Huang for more than a year.
From a securities perspective, Bartlett said, the company’s earlier statement was “clearly a misleading statement.” And because Huang is CEO, Bartlett said, “his knowledge gets imputed to the company.” In other words, Nvidia is treated as having known what its chief executive knew.
The Kistenmacher complaint makes the same argument.
Bartlett predicted a “classic fraud on the market” claim, in which investors argue they paid prices that reflected false or incomplete public information, and lost money when the truth emerged. This early lawsuit relies on that theory, and Monday’s drop of $7.97 per share, or 4.27%, gives the attorneys involved a lot to work with. Damages in such cases are tied to the stock’s decline, and Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world, so you can imagine a settlement could prove exceedingly expensive.
That means a large payment from the company and its directors-and-officers insurers, but typically no personal consequences for the CEO or the board. It is also a civil matter, so Huang isn’t facing prison over it. The irony, as Bartlett noted, is that the suit is brought in the name of Nvidia’s shareholders, and shareholders ultimately pay for the settlement, directly or through insurance premiums.
Bartlett sorted Nvidia’s wider exposure into buckets. The first is the securities fraud claim, which is the clearest immediate problem for the company and potentially for Huang. The second is governance: what the board knew and when. It’s possible directors were kept in the dark, but the board also has oversight duties, and once the Times began reporting on the Megaspeed connection, the company should have had reporting lines to bring a critical risk like this to directors. If it didn’t, or if directors didn’t act, board-level liability is possible.
A third category, one that would change everything, would arise only if the board’s investigation finds Huang knew about the intelligence connection. That would be “a whole other ball game,” as Bartlett said. (The board said in a statement to the public Sunday that it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.)
There’s also the question of government action. The SEC can seek an officer-and-director bar for intentional securities-fraud violations, which Bartlett said is technically on the table. But he doubts the current SEC under Chairman Paul Atkins would have the appetite, given President Trump’s support for Huang. A roughly two-year clock after discovery of the facts would leave room for a future administration to act, but the window would be tight, and Bartlett posited that’s pretty unlikely when asked about it.
It’s worth underscoring that neither law firm announcements nor this newly filed complaint is a sign of a strong case. Plaintiffs’ firms are quick to publish these notices when they see an opportunity. Which firm winds up leading the case is decided later by the court, and that decision usually depends on which investor has suffered the biggest loss. Kistenmacher said in his filing that he’s willing to serve as lead plaintiff, but the court will ultimately choose among the competing investors. No doubt they’ll materialize soon.

articles.title: AI hardware startup Nominal triples valuation to $3B in 8 months
articles.body:
Nominal, a four-year-old, Austin-based startup that offers an AI platform purpose-built for engineering and testing complex hardware, like aircraft, nuclear reactors, and smart factories, has raised another big round of financing that triples its valuation. On Monday, it announced a $240 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and co-led by Insight Partners.
This follows the company’s announcement in March of a $155 million Series B extension at a $1 billion valuation, led by Trae Stephens at Founders Fund. That round was a “preemptive” deal — meaning an offer initiated by the investor, not the startup. Other investors in the company include Sequoia, General Catalyst, and Lux Capital.
Nominal says that it has 80 commercial and government organizations as customers. One of its key customers is Anduril, the defense company co-founded by Stephens. Nominal also won a government contract in October when the Air Force selected it for a $71.2 million Strategic Funding Increase (STRATFI) investment, which is a program that requires matching funds from outside the Air Force.
Nominal CEO and co-founder Cameron McCord (pictured) is a former U.S. Navy submarine officer and an Anduril alum.

articles.title: Show HN: STE80 Humanizer – de-AI text by writing 80% of the way to ASD-STE100
articles.body:
STE80 Humanizer makes AI-written text read like a careful person wrote it, without changing what it says. It combines two methods:
- The humanizer method. Remove the 26 tells from Wikipedia's Signs of AI writing, in the catalog of blader/humanizer.
- Karpathy's STE80 method. Rebuild the sentences "80% of the way to ASD-STE100", the controlled English of aircraft maintenance manuals.
Before:
Great question! Kubernetes liveness probes are a powerful mechanism that enables the kubelet to determine whether a container is healthy — and it's not just a health check, it's your first line of defense. When a probe fails, the container will be automatically restarted by the kubelet, ensuring that your application remains available. However, it's important to note that misconfigured probes could potentially cause cascading restarts, so parameters like initialDelaySeconds and failureThreshold should be carefully tuned.
Get this right, and your cluster heals itself.
After:
A liveness probe tells the kubelet if a container is healthy. If the probe fails, the kubelet restarts the container. This keeps the application available.
A bad probe can also cause many restarts. For example, a timeout that is too short makes healthy containers fail the probe. To prevent this, set initialDelaySeconds and failureThreshold to values that fit your application.
The goal is text that people read easily. Getting past AI detectors is not a goal.
Most humanizers only remove phrases. The text loses "Great question!" and "seamless", but it keeps long sentences that carry three ideas, hide the actor and stack hedges. It still reads like AI. You can see it in the worked example in SKILL.md:
On 2 October 2026, Andrej Karpathy posted tips for one problem: as LLMs do more of the work, people spend more time reading and understanding what the models produce. His first tip:
Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent.
The post then goes up a ladder: diagrams, then HTML pages, then explainer videos. His conclusion is that our work moves "up the abstractions into oversight and understanding". Clear output is the bottleneck, and writing is the first step.
The STE overview graphic from Karpathy's post. Click to enlarge. Note: a later fact check found errors in the dictionary panel (D). In ASD-STE100 Issue 9, "approximately" is approved, "TEST" is approved only as a noun (not as a verb), and there is no entry for "in order to". This skill follows Issue 9.
ASD-STE100 (Simplified Technical English) is from the 1980s aerospace industry. It was made for mechanics whose first language is not English, because a misread step on an aircraft can kill. Its rules:
- 20 words per instruction and 25 per description
- one instruction per sentence
- active voice and simple tenses
- one meaning per word, with about 900 approved words
- one topic per paragraph, and six sentences at most
Why "80%"? At 100%, "check" and "test" are nouns only, "may" and "should" are banned and many common words are not allowed. Normal prose sounds stiff. At 80%, you keep the full structure and only as much vocabulary as still sounds natural:
Karpathy talks about readability, not about sounding human. This skill adds that part, because the two methods cover each other's gaps.
SKILL.md has two numbered lists:
- §1 to §26: the AI tells (Pass 1).
- S1 to S15: the STE80 structure rules (Pass 2).
Every entry has the same fields: Watch for, Problem, Before and After. Pass 2 entries also say what changes between 80% and Strict. Weak alone means: act only if other tells are near. The skill reports its edits by number, for example "§1, §8, S2", so you can look each one up.
Once installed, the skill answers to /ste80-humanizer. It also starts by itself when you ask to humanize, simplify or de-AI a text, or ask for STE.
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer
Global install for one agent, or for all of them:
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent claude-code
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent codex
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent cursor
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent '*'

articles.title: Show HN: STE80 Humanizer – de-AI text by writing 80% of the way to ASD-STE100
articles.body:
STE80 Humanizer makes AI-written text read like a careful person wrote it, without changing what it says. It combines two methods:
- The humanizer method. Remove the 26 tells from Wikipedia's Signs of AI writing, in the catalog of blader/humanizer.
- Karpathy's STE80 method. Rebuild the sentences "80% of the way to ASD-STE100", the controlled English of aircraft maintenance manuals.
Before:
Great question! Kubernetes liveness probes are a powerful mechanism that enables the kubelet to determine whether a container is healthy — and it's not just a health check, it's your first line of defense. When a probe fails, the container will be automatically restarted by the kubelet, ensuring that your application remains available. However, it's important to note that misconfigured probes could potentially cause cascading restarts, so parameters like initialDelaySeconds and failureThreshold should be carefully tuned.
Get this right, and your cluster heals itself.
After:
A liveness probe tells the kubelet if a container is healthy. If the probe fails, the kubelet restarts the container. This keeps the application available.
A bad probe can also cause many restarts. For example, a timeout that is too short makes healthy containers fail the probe. To prevent this, set initialDelaySeconds and failureThreshold to values that fit your application.
The goal is text that people read easily. Getting past AI detectors is not a goal.
Most humanizers only remove phrases. The text loses "Great question!" and "seamless", but it keeps long sentences that carry three ideas, hide the actor and stack hedges. It still reads like AI. You can see it in the worked example in SKILL.md:
On 2 October 2026, Andrej Karpathy posted tips for one problem: as LLMs do more of the work, people spend more time reading and understanding what the models produce. His first tip:
Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent.
The post then goes up a ladder: diagrams, then HTML pages, then explainer videos. His conclusion is that our work moves "up the abstractions into oversight and understanding". Clear output is the bottleneck, and writing is the first step.
The STE overview graphic from Karpathy's post. Click to enlarge. Note: a later fact check found errors in the dictionary panel (D). In ASD-STE100 Issue 9, "approximately" is approved, "TEST" is approved only as a noun (not as a verb), and there is no entry for "in order to". This skill follows Issue 9.
ASD-STE100 (Simplified Technical English) is from the 1980s aerospace industry. It was made for mechanics whose first language is not English, because a misread step on an aircraft can kill. Its rules:
- 20 words per instruction and 25 per description
- one instruction per sentence
- active voice and simple tenses
- one meaning per word, with about 900 approved words
- one topic per paragraph, and six sentences at most
Why "80%"? At 100%, "check" and "test" are nouns only, "may" and "should" are banned and many common words are not allowed. Normal prose sounds stiff. At 80%, you keep the full structure and only as much vocabulary as still sounds natural:
Karpathy talks about readability, not about sounding human. This skill adds that part, because the two methods cover each other's gaps.
SKILL.md has two numbered lists:
- §1 to §26: the AI tells (Pass 1).
- S1 to S15: the STE80 structure rules (Pass 2).
Every entry has the same fields: Watch for, Problem, Before and After. Pass 2 entries also say what changes between 80% and Strict. Weak alone means: act only if other tells are near. The skill reports its edits by number, for example "§1, §8, S2", so you can look each one up.
