Google Unveils Two New Specialized AI Chips to Widen Its Challenge to Nvidia
articles.body:
Google Unveils Two New Specialized AI Chips to Widen Its Challenge to Nvidia 11
			
		 	
				Google is expanding its AI chip lineup with two specialized TPUs arriving next year: the TPU 8tx, which encrypts sensitive data at the chip level for confidential computing, and the TPU 8i Max, which combines two TPU chips to provide more processing power and memory for long-context workloads. The move broadens Google's challenge to Nvidia as demand outstrips supply, with Google saying every TPU it currently has is already committed to customers. Quartz reports:  The 8tx is designed for sensitive, privacy-focused jobs run by clients including public-sector bodies and businesses in heavily regulated sectors, according to Bloomberg. It pairs with a central processing unit from Advanced Micro Devices and encrypts data at the chip level. Normally, data must be decrypted in memory as the machine works on it, [said Amin Vahdat, Chief Technologist for AI & Infrastructure at Google].
The 8i Max is meant for AI applications that need long context windows, meaning the volume of information a model can take into account within one request. Vahdat said that matters for drug discovery, math and coding. The chip packs two TPU chips together, giving it extra processing muscle and memory.
Both variations are reconfigured versions of existing silicon rather than new designs, Vahdat said. Google changed them to handle tasks customers have requested. They follow two TPU models Google released this year, according to Bloomberg, which said the chip unit used to release one new processor every two years. "We could build a single chip that tries to address the whole market, or by building specialized versions of the chips, we actually can deliver much more value," Vahdat said, according to Bloomberg.

articles.title: Son Lux’s Music Video for ‘Out Into Us’ Is an Atmospheric Foray Between Past and Present
articles.body:
Son Lux’s Music Video for ‘Out Into Us’ Is an Atmospheric Foray Between Past and Present
Son Lux’s newest music video is an atmospheric mini-epic. Last month, the video premiered at MASS MoCA—the piece is a joint commission by the museum and Pioneer Works and made in collaboration with Alex Cook—as an immersive, 17-minute installation titled “Out Into Us (Slow Down),” complementing the release of the band’s ninth studio album.
“In the last decade, social media has created a reality in which music is often eclipsed by visuals, served up in an endless buffet of bite-sized and contextless flavors,” says a statement. For this multimedia work, the artists leaned instead toward deeply felt human experiences, like how long it can take to do or understand something. Portraying a multigenerational family seated around a table and passing the time in one another’s company, the video transports us back at least a century as scenes of a giant dust cloud evoke the Dust Bowl.
Cook conjures tension, atmosphere, and moments of disrupted reality in a slippage of past and present. The Dust Bowl itself was inherently linked to an intense period when homesteaders, dreaming of prosperous lives for themselves, plowed vast swaths of prairie for their farms. In the process, they uprooted native grasses that held the topsoil in place. Then, exacerbated by drought, millions of acres of topsoil eroded completely from the Great Plains’ persistent and powerful winds, sending farms and habitats into ruin.
Taking surprisingly meta turns, the the sound and visuals provoke curiosity, togetherness, hope, and grief. The family passes delicious dishes around the table and works on a puzzle depicting an idealized landscape in the tradition of the Hudson River School—a far cry from their depicted reality, yet a type of historical propaganda that helped entice homesteaders to the plains. These bucolic tableaux and their romantic ideals could even be said to have functioned something like social media does today, as a way to spread information. Instead, Cook and Son Lux confront us—watch to the end—with quite another definition of a screen.
“Sound can create a sanctuary—a space in which we can remember what it feels like to be present in our bodies and lost in our thoughts,” says the band’s guitarist, Rafiq Bhatia. “When you decrease the playback speed of a piece of music, you can really linger in its hidden corners and shadows: passing tensions and moments of release become whole rooms you can step into and stay for a while.”
See more on Cook’s Vimeo.

articles.title: Reddit Founder Says Building Social Media Apps Is 'Not Cool Anymore'
articles.body:
Reddit Founder Says Building Social Media Apps Is 'Not Cool Anymore' (wired.com) 38
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Alexis Ohanian wants to figure out the future of user-generated content. According to the Reddit cofounder, building social media apps is "not cool anymore" and so much of the internet has been compromised. "I'm expecting some better version of the group chat to be that new version of UGC," Ohanian told WIRED senior correspondent Lauren Goode at the inaugural WIRED World Fair. [...] Ohanian is a proponent of the "Dead Internet Theory"—the idea that a lot of online activity and content is being generated by bots. Large language models have turbocharged this, with AI agents outrunning human users. "The internet that I grew up on  that was really built for humans first; user interfaces and experiences are going to go away," said Ohanian, "because more of the internet is going to get created for these agents to use, [rather] than for people."
In some ways, the advance in generative AI has been lucrative for sites like Reddit, which has licensed its vast archive of human conversations to companies including Google and OpenAI to train AI models. "Platforms like ours became very, very valuable to LLMs," Ohanian said. But the technology has also undermined the business. Reddit shares plunged 29 percent last week after the platform warned that Google's AI-powered search was hurting referral traffic. Ohanian also worries the commercialization of these conversations means they are full of "bullshit." "The internet has gotten so manipulated because it is so incredibly valuable to do so," he said.
Reddit recently said it would require users to sign in to fight third-party scraping and keep up user engagement. While Ohanian declined to say whether he agrees with the move, "there has to be provable humanity on the internet without being creepy."  An early Anthropic investor, Ohanian is nonetheless optimistic about the potential benefits of AI. He is especially excited to see medical breakthroughs from the technology. "There is still a very real chance that this technology can cause a lot of harm for sure," he said. "I think we have to be sober about how we're building and what we're doing, but I still can't help but see all of the things that can get so demonstrably better."

articles.title: How to shop like a pro during Black Friday and Cyber Monday
articles.body:
Despite Amazon and other retailers filling the summer and fall months with more sales than ever before, Black Friday and Cyber Monday remain the biggest shopping days of the year. And, in recent years, the sale periods have started earlier, giving you more time to take advantage of the deals.
How to shop like a pro during Black Friday and Cyber Monday
The annual deal extravaganza can be overwhelming, but the right tool and a little patience can help you score big.
We’re already hard at work to find the best prices on phones, accessories, 4K TVs, noise-canceling headphones, gaming gear, and other tech throughout the deal-packed weeks culminating in the big events, whether you plan to shop in person or online.
You can always count on us to publish only the best deals that you need to know about, no matter the season. However, if you want to be among the first people to spot price drops on the products you’re interested in, you’ll want to get a head start on your Black Friday and Cyber Monday game plan. Thankfully, we have a few suggestions for scouting early sales at your favorite retailers, finding the right price-tracking tool, and setting up email alerts to ensure you don’t miss rare discounts at Amazon and elsewhere.
Leverage a price-tracking tool or deal aggregator
The most effective way to find a truly great deal is to set up a price-tracking tool. We’ve included a few of our favorites below, many of which we use daily here at The Verge. Each can help you track deals at various retailers — including Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, and Target — but they each do so differently and come with their own set of advantages / disadvantages.
All of them are free to use, and once you’ve added the products you’re interested in keeping an eye on, you can rest easy knowing that you don’t need to take any action until it comes time to make a purchase. Just make sure you keep your email notifications on so you see the alerts as they come in.
CamelCamelCamel is arguably the most popular price-tracking tool at The Verge, and for good reason: it’s incredibly useful since it tracks the price of every product sold on Amazon and can send you alerts when an item falls to a customizable price threshold. Once a product reaches the desired price you’ve set (or lower), you’ll get an email about it. You can use the extension’s price graph to determine what price is likely to happen based on historical data, but it’s always a shot in the dark.
To track prices and get alerts via email, you’ll need to create a free CamelCamelCamel account. Additionally, we suggest installing the site’s browser extension, The Camelizer, which works with Google Chrome, Safari, Mozilla Firefox, Opera, and Microsoft Edge. The handy tool lets you view pricing trends on a product-by-product basis and set your desired price without leaving Amazon. It’s fantastic, easy to use, and works in several countries, including the US, UK, Canada, Germany, Spain, France, Italy, and Australia.
As mentioned, the tracker only works for products listed on Amazon. However, in May, the company released CamelMart, its price tracker for Walmart. While it doesn’t have a browser extension (yet), its functionality is similar to CamelCamelCamel in that you can set price alerts and email notifications, so you’ll always know when your desired price threshold for a particular product is met.
Like CamelCamelCamel, Keepa is another handy tool for tracking product prices on Amazon. Keepa has charts that track pricing trends and can alert you when it finds a deal. Similarly, you can also import any of your Amazon wishlists.
Unlike CamelCamelCamel, however, you don’t necessarily need to create an account to track prices with Keepa; just install the appropriate browser extension for Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Firefox, or Opera, and Keepa will automatically add a price history graph to supported product listings. The embedded graph shows pricing history and allows you to specify various pricing details. If you set a desired price, Keepa will send you a price alert via email, push notification, Telegram, or RSS.
Slickdeals aggregates some of the best deals around the internet, as discovered by its team and community of users. Its site also lets you browse coupons and create deal alerts based on specific keywords, though the latter works a little differently on Slickdeals than it does with the sites above.
You can type in a product name, like “Nintendo Switch 2,” “OLED TVs,” or a retailer’s name, and once it’s added to your list, you’ll get a deal alert if it meets your criteria. You can set it to alert you to literally any deal related to your keyword, or you can filter out deals so you’ll only be notified if, for example, the deal is popular enough to make it to Slickdeals’ front page or earns a high rating from the community. If you like browsing deals, it’s generally a good idea to visit Slickdeals frequently, especially since it usually has a Black Friday component that allows you to browse circulars for Best Buy, Target, and other retailers in advance.
Also, it’s just fun to see what the community digs up.
For a more hands-off way to see whether you’re getting a good deal, try your browser’s built-in tools. For a few years now, Edge has been able to tell you when you’re looking at the best price for a particular product from a range of retailers, and Google Chrome can track price fluctuations and notify you when a particular product goes on sale. Edge and Chrome are available on Windows, macOS, and Linux, as well as Android and iOS.
Use Alexa for Shopping, Amazon’s capable AI chatbot
You may have already noticed that sometimes, when you’re shopping on Amazon, a sidebar opens to reveal more information about the product you’re looking at. Even if you haven’t used it, you can’t miss it; it’s prominently featured in Amazon’s upper nav bar and accessible by clicking the Price History button on a given listing.
Whether you’re using the Amazon app or the website, it’s a capable tool that, at its core, does some of the same tasks as our other recommendations. It can send price alerts and show up to a year’s worth of pricing data, helping you make informed buying decisions for products on Amazon. It can also recommend alternatives that might be a better value and, if you’ll allow it, can even automatically purchase products on your behalf.
It can do a lot more, too. For instance, you can have it update you when, say, a specific product launches, and it can shop on your behalf by adding specified items to your cart at a specified frequency. You can also use it to compare products sold on Amazon, and even upload photos of wishlists to find matching products.
Set up deal alerts for Alexa or the Amazon app
If you have an Alexa-compatible smart gadget, such as an older Echo Dot Max or one of the company’s newer Echo devices, you can ask the virtual assistant to alert you when specific products go on sale. You can receive alerts up to 24 hours in advance of planned price drops for eligible products, or as soon as it notices a discount on anything saved in your shopping cart or wish list. If you say, “Alexa, buy it for me,” after being notified of the deal, the assistant will purchase the item for you once the discount becomes available.
To enable these features, open the Alexa app on your smartphone and navigate to More > Settings > Notifications > Amazon Shopping. Then, toggle the slider next to Deal Recommendations within the Shopping Recommendations section. Alexa will audibly notify you of deals moving forward, but if you happen to miss one, you can check for the notification on your phone or see whether you have any new notifications on an Echo device by checking for the yellow light. If it’s lit, just say, “Alexa, play notifications.”
You can receive similar notifications on your smartphone from the Amazon Shopping app, too. Just open the app and go to Settings > Notifications > Deals and recommendations, and toggle the slider next to the Savings option.
Check retailer schedules and plan for early shopping events
Keeping an eye on preferred retailers before Black Friday will help save you time (and money). Several major retailers have already detailed their plans in the run-up to the holidays, and many will offer early opportunities to save. For example:
- Walmart is hosting three online shopping events for Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Its first event runs from November 12th through the 15th, serving as a preview of sorts. The second runs from November 23rd to the 29th, encapsulating Black Friday and the days surrounding it. Finally, it switches to Cyber Monday on November 30th, with deals lasting through December 2nd. Walmart Plus customers get a 24-hour lead on deals, as in previous years, and any remaining deals will open to all customers afterward. In-store events are also scheduled for November 12th through the 15th, as well as November 27th (Black Friday), each starting at 6AM local time. Walmart’s Cyber Monday deals are online-only and start at 12:01AM ET.
- Target is going all in on early shopping this year, with a three-day shopping event happening from November 5th through the 7th, with new limited-time offers every weekend. The retailer will also host a new “Deal of the Day” each day through December 24th.
- Best Buy kicked off its early Black Friday event on Friday, October 30th. That’s done, but it’s continuing with deal events throughout the year. New doorbuster deals will drop every Friday, and its first early Black Friday event starts on November 6th. The retailer’s extended Black Friday sale will begin immediately afterward on November 19th and run through the 28th, offering a chance to save on previous doorbusters and some Black Friday exclusives. It’ll then transition into a two-day Cyber Monday sale, which will take place on November 29th and November 30th. Finally, it’ll host a “last-minute savings event” between December 18th and the 24th.
You can expect more major retailers to detail their Black Friday plans shortly, so keep an eye on their respective websites and start filling your calendar accordingly.
Pay close attention to lightning deals and doorbusters
Doorbusters, lightning deals, and other limited-time discounts are a tried-and-true hallmark of any Black Friday sale. They’ll usually be the most buzzworthy deals you’ll see all year, with truly low prices to spark impulsive spending. As you’re checking ads, make a note of these deals and read all of the fine print surrounding their availability. Some may require you to sign up in advance or get in line early (ahem, Amazon), and some can be so scarce that you won’t have the entire weekend — or even an hour — to claim them.
Have a price-matching backup plan
Although many stores will automatically match their competitors’ pricing, sometimes you may need to twist their arm. It’s helpful to know the various price-matching policies of each retailer in the event that your preferred store runs out of stock on certain goods. You can get up to speed with our price-matching guide, which details the lengths each retailer will or won’t go to win your dollar. Unfortunately, some retailers put a temporary halt on their usual policies during special shopping events like Black Friday, but it never hurts to ask.
Trust the experts
We’re a discerning bunch here at The Verge, so don’t fret if you’re going into Black Friday and Cyber Monday without any prep. We’ll be corralling the best tech deals and keeping our coverage up to date with new sale items while dropping old ones to avoid disappointment. While we usually suggest paying attention to deals starting the day after Thanksgiving — or November 27th, in this case — the truth is that several retailers typically jump the gun and start offering some great deals in the lead-up to the shopping holiday.
To catch every opportunity to save, be sure to bookmark our coverage, follow us on Bluesky, subscribe to our weekday Verge Deals newsletter, and start setting aside some cash for Black Friday and Cyber Monday.
Update 10:00AM ET, November 9th: We’ve added new ways to track prices for the upcoming 2026 holiday shopping season.

articles.title: Torrent underground
articles.body:
When Jane first heard about Memory and Imagination, a rare 1990s documentary about the Library of Congress, she was intrigued. But the Canadian writer in her 30s couldn’t find the movie anywhere — not on streaming services, not on YouTube, not on pirate sites — and her intrigue turned into obsession.
Torrent underground
Inside the exclusive world of private torrent trackers — and the everyday people behind the piracy boom.
by Janko Roettgers
Illustrations: Lorenzo Matteuci for The Verge, Animation by Verge Staff
Worried it might become a lost film, Jane decided to scour auction sites, search every library catalog she could think of, and even enlist some of her online acquaintances to find a copy. Her plan was to “share it with other people to help ensure it would be preserved into the future,” as she puts it. Jane knew the perfect tool for the task: a private torrent tracker.
“I am ethically conflicted about piracy. I often feel guilty about it.”
Private trackers are essentially the speakeasies of the online piracy world. Promoted primarily by word of mouth, they rely on secrecy, exclusivity, and strict community rules to shield everything that’s going on behind closed doors from the public’s prying eyes. What unites these communities is that they all use BitTorrent to trade media among like-minded file sharers. But their focuses range widely, from general-purpose trackers with catalogs so broad that they make Netflix look like a niche service to the many specialized communities for categories like Chinese movies, motorsports, visual effects tools, e-learning courses, and Japanese porn. There’s even a private tracker just for Frank Zappa music.
Private trackers are known for massive and meticulously organized catalogs, which they owe to users like Jane, who, like every other pirate I talked to for this story, opted to be identified by a pseudonym due to the terabytes of copyrighted data they’ve been sharing. These are people willing to go the extra mile to find long-forgotten movies, rare concert recordings, or out-of-print books. “Many private tracker users are fully consumed with archive fever,” she says.
At first, Jane had no luck finding a physical copy of that elusive documentary, which includes interviews with Steve Jobs and Julia Child. Nobody was selling it on eBay. Her local public library didn’t have it. Neither did any other public library in North America. And when she finally located a DVD that was available to the public, it was in the Bibliotheca Alexandrina — Egypt’s modern-day re-creation of the ancient library that’s long been synonymous with lost media. “That bowled me over,” Jane says. “This obscure movie I’m looking for is only available in the Library of Alexandria!”
Eventually, Jane found Memory and Imagination for sale on a small online marketplace for historical media. Jane instantly bought a copy and uploaded it. “It looked like a digital rip of a severely degraded VHS tape,” she says. “I was still over the moon [that] I rescued this historically significant documentary.”
Not everyone who uses private trackers shares Jane’s amateur-archivist zeal. Some are simply in it for easy access to pirated movies, TV shows, or other forms of entertainment. “My goal initially was to have a better source for video games,” says Odel, a West Coast-based college student. “I quickly found out that [private trackers] could replace everything else.” Others join trackers in search of a community of like-minded cinephiles or music fans. And as they immerse themselves in a world of illicit media trading that’s largely shielded from public view, many of them seem to catch a peculiar kind of bug.
“There aren’t many closed doors on the internet.”
They painstakingly work their way up the ranks in the trackers they’ve joined and then use their freshly earned social capital to get access to even more exclusive sites, where the same rat race starts all over again. “Exclusivity definitely plays a part,” says Maysay, a private tracker user from Pakistan. “You want to get into those more exclusive ‘elite’ trackers at some point just for the sake of it.”
“There is definitely a constant quest to level up,” says Jane, who maintains active accounts on 14 private trackers.
Among the people I talked to for this story, that’s actually a small number. Some private tracker users maintain dozens of accounts, download terabytes of data, share thousands of torrents at a time, embark on obsessive quests to get their hands on long-lost media, and use automated apps and tools that make everyday piracy seem like child’s play.
In a world where streaming services offer access to countless movies and TV shows for little more than your credit card number, private trackers can seem a bit like a throwback. A nod to a different time, when legal options didn’t really exist and file sharing happened in private chat rooms or on password-protected FTP servers.
“There aren’t many closed doors on the internet,” says Jane, who became interested in joining private trackers after hearing about them from friends. Jane quickly realized that she couldn’t just sign up for the latest and greatest movie trackers, which were only open to vetted users with a history of good behavior on other servers. So she devised a plan to join a more lenient private tracker for audiobooks first and work her way up from there.
Users who fall below certain metrics often find their download privileges curtailed, and especially egregious offenses result in instant bans.
Even getting access to that first server came with some hurdles. Private tracker websites rarely have freely accessible sign-up forms. Some only open their doors to new users every few weeks or months, while others use special vetting processes to make sure applicants are a good fit. Sometimes this means that applicants are required to prove they’re in good standing on other trackers. Sometimes they need to take screenshots of their personal media collections to show they’re actually interested in what the tracker they’re applying to is all about. And sometimes there are even actual interviews applicants have to ace before getting their accounts.
The long-defunct private music tracker What.CD used to quiz applicants about audio formats and MP3 encoder settings, and even published a study guide of sorts to help them prepare for it. And Jane’s very first private tracker required her to first join an IRC chatroom, where admins quizzed her about the server’s rules. “It was so stressful! It felt like a job interview,” she says.
Not every private tracker has these kinds of interviews, but like Jane’s first server, most are big on rules. Users are generally required to keep up a certain upload-to-download ratio, with many sites demanding that they contribute as much bandwidth as they consume. (The exact rules and requirements vary, and many trackers also offer some “freeleech” content — files that can be downloaded without negatively impacting a user’s ratio.) Quickly downloading a file without sharing it is also frowned upon, as is the unvetted distribution of invites to outsiders.
Users who fall below certain metrics often find their download privileges curtailed, and especially egregious offenses result in instant bans. “Invite selling is considered to be a major breach of security,” says Odel. Doing so will not only get you kicked from a server, it will also tarnish your reputation elsewhere. “Staff of the tracker you did it on will typically communicate with the staff of some other trackers, which can result in you getting banned from those places as well,” Odel explains.
If you do follow the rules and share generously, you have a chance to work your way up the ranks, which then opens the doors to other trackers. That alone, and the requirement to keep up a healthy upload-to-download ratio, can lead to people downloading and then redistributing (also known as “seeding” in tracker lingo) files just to maintain their stats. “Some places will require you to seed [a certain amount of] terabytes before you get access to a certain rank,” says Odel. “This can result in a lot of downloading of stuff I wouldn’t ever consume otherwise, just to pump up that number.”
“You have to seed things you aren’t interested in consuming to succeed in the tracker economy.”
Odel estimates that he has downloaded around 500 terabytes of data from the 30 or so private trackers he’s currently active on. In the end, he’s watched very little of it. “Probably less than one percent,” he says.
That discrepancy is not uncommon. “I am seeding over 2,000 torrents, and I have no personal interest in almost any of them,” admits Jane. Maysay tells me that he seeds around 3,000 torrents at any given time and has downloaded things he doesn’t intend to watch “many times.”
“It’s how these sites are built,” Jane explains. “You have to seed things you aren’t interested in consuming to succeed in the tracker economy.” Some private tracker users use automated tools to help them maintain their ratio, like scripts that watch dedicated IRC channels to quickly jump on any newly released torrent, no matter what content it is. This is called “racing” in tracker lingo, and it can help improve one’s ratio; anyone looking to download that file later will get it from those early downloaders. Especially committed users even rent a dedicated seedbox — a private server sitting in some remote data center that is only used for downloading and then seeding torrents.
Being able to download more is only one reason for trying to improve your ratio and standing on private trackers. “I just do it for fun,” Jane says. “It’s kind of like playing a video game and watching your score go up.” And just like with some video games, there is a certain addictive quality to all this. ”Using private trackers reminded me a lot of playing MMORPG games like World of Warcraft or RuneScape where you really have to grind to level up,” Jane says. “It’s slow, tedious, and repetitive. Yet you feel this insatiable compulsion to level up.”
Private BitTorrent trackers emerged soon after BitTorrent itself was created 25 years ago. This was at the height of the file-sharing wars, when Hollywood and the major record labels were taking one peer-to-peer network operator after another to court. Entertainment industry lawsuits resulted in the shutdown of Napster in 2001, Audiogalaxy in 2002, and Kazaa in 2006.
Those closures drove millions of file sharers to embrace BitTorrent, which in turn put torrent sites into the crosshairs of rightsholders and their lawyers. Suprnova, a public torrent site frequented by millions of users, shut down amid legal pressure at the end of 2004. And in 2006, authorities raided The Pirate Bay.
Some torrent site admins responded to the increasing legal pressure by simply pulling up a drawbridge to their piracy communities. Instead of letting just anyone download torrents, they required users to register, and in some cases only admitted new users that had gotten an invite from a trusted community member.
Nobody knows exactly how many private trackers are currently up and running, or how many people use them for their pirated media fix. But while BitTorrent piracy as a whole has declined since the emergence of Netflix, Spotify, and other paid streaming services, private trackers are still going strong.
A live dashboard maintained by a tracker software developer currently lists around 530 private trackers, including some with hundreds of thousands of registered users. One music tracker, listed only as [REDACTED] on this dashboard, is said to host 3.7 million torrents, or works to download. A popular movie tracker included in the list has more than 1 million torrents, which are being traded among just 40,000 registered users.
“Occasionally people will request or ask for something that just isn’t available commercially anymore, or ever, and attach a huge bounty to it.”
One of the first notable private trackers was Oink’s Pink Palace, an invite-only music sharing community with a reported 180,000 registered users. Among them was Nine Inch Nails front man Trent Reznor, who told Vulture in 2007 that the site had been “like the world’s greatest record store,” offering access to “pretty much anything you could ever imagine [...] in the format you wanted.”
Many private tracker communities meticulously curate catalogs that put publicly accessible piracy sites to shame. “The private tracker experience is a lot better,” says Marvin, a 23-year-old software developer from the Pacific Northwest. Public torrent sites are often ad-ridden and hard to navigate and search, he says. Maysay agrees, telling me that he appreciates private trackers “not just because of the amount of content [available], but also because of the quality, organization, and how well everything is sorted.”
The curation happening in these private communities is very much a group effort. Many private trackers offer their members a chance to request files they want others to upload, complete with bounties (download credits that you would otherwise have to upload other files for) for the first uploader. The rarer the file, the bigger the bounty. And the bigger the bounty, the more frenzied the hunt for that elusive file.
”Are large corporations to be trusted with archiving our culture?”
One famous quest for such a bounty unfolded in 2013, when a user of the since-shuttered What.CD server put out a request for “The Ocean Full of Bowling Balls,” a story from Catcher in the Rye author J.D. Salinger that the writer himself had refused to publish. For a long time, the only known copy of “The Ocean Full of Bowling Balls” resided in Princeton University’s Firestone Library, where visitors could read but not copy the document.
The intrigue — Salinger didn’t publish a single work for the last 45 years of his life — combined with the fact that there clearly was at least one copy out there set off a frenzy among What.CD users, with the bounty reportedly swelling to a massive 6TB. Some came up with schemes to memorize every word of the story while visiting Princeton’s library, while others scoured the Earth for other copies.
A few months later, a What.CD user was ready to claim the bounty. “It took me many weeks of research to find that this book existed and many more weeks to acquire it,” the user wrote in a note accompanying a torrent featuring a total of three unpublished Salinger stories, including “The Ocean Full of Bowling Balls.” Someone had apparently published the three stories as part of a book that was printed just 25 times in 1999. Years later, one of those 25 copies showed up on eBay, where the What.CD uploader quickly snagged it.
The story of this unlikely act of renegade archiving quickly made headlines worldwide, and to this day is legendary in the private tracker community. (The uploader of the book was ironically never able to claim their massive bounty, as site admins removed the torrent once it got too much outside attention.) But while few other bounty hunts have gotten that much attention, they do happen.
“A great deal of media released today will persist via private servers, much like how a lot of silent films we have today were found as reels stored in people’s attics.”
“Occasionally people will request or ask for something that just isn’t available commercially anymore, or ever, and attach a huge bounty to it,” says Odel. “People will research any potential leads, reach out to random French directors via email, and ultimately come back with nothing. Then, a few years later, somebody will randomly upload whatever was being looked for onto YouTube, with no further explanation.”
Odel told me he doesn’t personally partake in these kinds of media hunts. “But I’ve seen some things which I’d classify as ‘important’ be recovered this way,” he says. “Piracy does happen to be pretty good at preservation.”
UC Berkeley professor Abigail De Kosnik, who has investigated private trackers as part of her research on rogue online archives, agrees. “A great deal of media released today will persist via private servers, much like how a lot of silent films we have today were found as reels stored in people’s attics,” she says. “I think that private torrent trackers, which make possible [to download] many art films, indie films, smaller-budget films, films from many countries, will play a large part in constituting future archives of 20th and 21st century cultural productions.”
Copyright holders, unsurprisingly, often hold less favorable views of the private tracker community. “Private trackers are part of a broader piracy ecosystem,” says Larissa Knapp, executive vice president and chief content protection officer of the Motion Picture Association (MPA). “Content that first appears within a closed community can quickly migrate to streaming sites, cyberlockers, IPTV services, and other unauthorized platforms, significantly amplifying its reach and impact.”
Rightsholder groups have repeatedly gone after private trackers and their administrators with varying levels of success. Oink’s Pink Palace, the popular private music tracker, shut down in 2007 following raids in the Netherlands and the UK. Oink admin Alan Ellis was arrested and charged with conspiracy to defraud as part of the enforcement actions, but was later found not guilty in court. Shuttering the tracker also did little to stop file sharing. Oink was quickly succeeded by What.CD, which remained online for nearly a decade until finally closing down in 2016 following a raid on its data center.
These days, private file sharing communities aren’t as often in the news as they were a decade ago. Part of that is simply a matter of priority. Private trackers often cap the number of registered users; some of the most coveted communities have only 40,000 or fewer active members. Public sites like The Pirate Bay, on the other hand, still attract millions of file sharers, making it easier for commercial copyright enforcers to send out tens of thousands of legal notices to end users at a time — a practice that’s especially common in Europe.
Still, groups like the MPA, and its ACE anti-piracy arm, haven’t given up on going after private file sharing communities and their admins. “Private trackers are not beyond enforcement reach,” Knapp says. “Closed access can make an investigation more difficult, but it does not eliminate the legal or operational exposure for the people who run them. In my years in federal law enforcement, I learned that anonymity is rarely as complete as people believe. A private community is not a safe harbor. Every operation, no matter how closed, still depends on people, hosting and domain services, communications tools, and usually some way to move money. Each of those is a connection, and connections are what investigators follow.”
There’s also the moral questions of engaging in piracy, which don’t get easier to answer when you’re actively sharing thousands of files 24/7. “I am ethically conflicted about piracy,” Jane says. “I often feel guilty about it.” Jane tries to assuage some of her guilt by actively purchasing media she likes.
Others told me a similar version of this, while also stressing that piracy is simply more user-friendly and convenient than legal services. That’s especially true for users in developing countries. “A big part of it for me is accessibility,” says Maysay, whose choices in Pakistan are limited. “There’s a lot of content that simply isn’t easily available legally here.”
“In my years in federal law enforcement, I learned that anonymity is rarely as complete as people believe.”
The fast-moving copyright battle around AI adds further ambiguity to this debate. “Now that the fastest-growing corner of the knowledge industries relies on mass piracy — copying huge amounts of data that they download for free — I think that the anti-piracy rhetoric of the past quarter-century is looking a bit outdated,” says De Kosnik. “If anything, AI [companies] are anti-archival because they strip away attribution from the creators, whereas private trackers are intensely accurate in providing details about the source material. So, are large corporations to be trusted with archiving our culture?”
Still, some of the users I spoke to were also acutely aware that it’s hard for them to take the moral high road. “It may genuinely hurt smaller creators,” Odel admits. “I’m not a fan of the people who try to advocate for it being moral or anything. I tend to justify my own piracy under the lense of ‘I wouldn’t be watching x otherwise.’ Whether that would be true assuming I was suddenly unable to pirate anything, I do not know.”
Not everyone is as conflicted about using private trackers. “I own it, it’s piracy. I torrent this content because I find it very convenient and don’t want to pay for every audiobook, TV episode, movie, etc.,” says Marvin.
Marvin tells me he originally got into piracy for financial reasons. “It was a habit that started with me growing up poor,” he says. Nowadays, that’s less of an issue for him, and he does spend money on some content, including books and video games.
“But I am a pirate at heart,” Marvin acknowledges. “This is paid content that I am getting for free. I’ve never paid for a subscription to a major streamer, and at this point, I don’t see why I ever would.”

articles.title: Trump’s 60 Minutes interview touched on AI safety, threat to arrest an AI exec
articles.body:
Asked about AI executives’ warnings about their models’ safety on 60 Minutes, Trump said, “I think that the risk is not nearly as real as it– as they talk, and I think the risk can be managed, and it’s managed.” He claimed the DOJ is managing that risk, saying, “We had a situation where somebody was reported to us to be doing something bad with AI. We called them very strongly and said, ‘Get ready to go to jail. Please give your wife a kiss good night.’”
Trump’s 60 Minutes interview touched on AI safety, threat to arrest an AI exec
Trump claims the DOJ told a top AI executive, ‘get ready to go to jail.’
Trump refused to name the person or company he was referring to, but said it was the leader of an AI company, “One of the big ones.” He claimed that after the threat of arrest, “this person totally changed everything.” Despite previously claiming that “artificial intelligence” is a term used by people he considers the enemy, Trump said AI rather than SI or super intelligence multiple times during the interview. Eventually he said China’s Xi is “…all in to SI, as I call it, because it really is super intelligence. It’s a much better name, I think, because it’s not artificial.”
60 Minutes’s Ross Douthat went on to ask if Trump would work with Democrats on AI safety, and Trump said he “absolutely would,” adding, “I don’t mind guardrails, but I don’t want to put us in a deep second position. We’re leading number one. And China has no guardrails, by the way. [...] They have the guardrails that whatever President Xi says goes. With me, it’s pretty strong, but it’s not quite that strong.”

articles.title: Parking-app convenience fees in 312 U.S. cities (median $0.35 per session)
articles.body:
Parking App Fees by City
Data checked Nov 5, 2026 · 314 rows · CC BY 4.0
Key findings
- Most common fees: $0.35 (108 places), $0.45 (56 places), $0.30 (30 places).
- Highest flat fee: $0.70 in Anchorage, AK.
- 15 places charge drivers no app fee.
- The data covers 312 places in 43 states and DC; 13 rows have no published fee.
Parking app fees by app company
Per-session fees in places where the fee is published, by the company that runs the app. Sources are listed at the bottom of the page.
Parking app fees by place
Every place in the data, by state. The source column names where each fee comes from and when that page was last updated or checked. A city name links to its Park Graph parking page when there is one.
Not published: no fee figure on the source page.
For parking lot owners
The fee in this report is paid by the driver, on top of your rate. Park Graph charges a per-transaction software fee on the operator side and does not add a separate convenience fee on the driver. Drivers scan the QR code on your sign and pay the rate you set, with no app to download. See Park Graph pricing for the fee on each plan, or compare Park Graph with the apps above:
Methodology
Park Graph collected the per-session fee a driver pays to start a parking session by app in each U.S. place where an app company or the city publishes it: ParkMobile, PayByPhone, Passport, Flowbird, Park Smarter and city-branded apps run by those companies. Sources are the app companies' own help pages and official city pages. Where a company page and a city page disagree, the CSV's fee_notes column says so.
A place with no published fee keeps its row, shown here as Not published. Membership plans the app companies offer, and their prices, are in the CSV's membership columns. Every row was checked on Nov 5, 2026.

Take QR-code payments at your lot with no hardware to install. You set your own prices.
Parking app fees FAQ
- How much does ParkMobile charge per parking session?
- Per ParkMobile's own help pages, its per-session fee runs from $0 to $0.75 depending on the city, with a median of $0.35 across 289 U.S. places, as of Nov 5, 2026. The fee is set place by place, so check the zone you park in.
- Is the app fee part of the parking rate?
- No. The app fee is charged per parking session on top of the parking rate, so the total you pay is the rate for your time plus the fee, per session.

- Yes. 15 places in this data charge drivers no app fee, including Burbank, CA; Union City, CA; Mountain Village, CO. Some cities also change the fee by how long you park or how you pay.

- No. Park Graph charges a per-transaction software fee on the operator side and does not add a separate convenience fee on the driver. Drivers pay the rate on the lot's sign.

- From the app companies' own help pages and from city parking pages, checked on Nov 5, 2026. 296 rows come from ParkMobile's help center, one article per city or zone. Each row's exact page is in the source_url column of the CSV.

articles.title: 6 Hours of YouTube and 85 handtyped pages of notes on LLM Inference – Start here
articles.body:
Teaching LLM inference from first principles by building a small engine in C++ and CUDA.
The series follows what happens between a prompt and a generated token, from loading model weights to running each part of the transformer on the GPU.
Read Inference from Scratch (PDF) for 80+ pages of my handwritten notes and diagrams. I developed all of the writing in this PDF myself, with NO AI writing.
Companion notes for every video are in the study-notes index, with separate Markdown and PDF folders. You can also read the complete PDF collection.
- A C++17 / CUDA project, built with CMake and linked with ICU for Unicode-aware tokenization.
- Direct model.safetensors loading: parse metadata, validate tensor offsets, and copy the raw BF16 weights to GPU memory. There is also a memory-mapped loader implementation to avoid an extra CPU-side copy.
- A fixed Llama 3.2 1B Instruct weight layout, with direct pointers to the embedding, normalization, attention, and MLP tensors across all 16 layers.
- A local BPE tokenizer that supports Unicode, special tokens, encode/decode, and the Instruct chat prompt format; its expected output is covered by a dedicated test executable.
- A CUDA embedding-gather kernel and prefill path that copies prompt token IDs to the GPU and allocates activations.
- A CUDA RMSNorm kernel for the 2,048-wide hidden state: it reduces in FP32 and applies the learned BF16 weights throughout the forward pass.
- Dense causal prefill now runs all 16 layers: Q/K/V projection, RoPE, grouped-query attention, output projection, the attention residual, post-attention RMSNorm, SwiGLU MLP, and the MLP residual.
- The final RMSNorm and tied embedding/LM-head projection produce FP32 logits; GPU argmax selects each next token.
- A shared BF16 KV page pool with a block table per sequence and layer. Each physical page holds 16 tokens of K and V; prefill fills prompt pages and decode appends one new token at its absolute RoPE position.
- Greedy response generation with Instruct chat formatting, end-of-turn/end-of-text stopping, and configurable output length within the 2,048-token context.
- Persistent scratch buffers and one cuBLAS handle shared by prefill and decode. Q storage is reused for output/MLP projections, and normalization storage is reused for attention output.
- Batched decode with runtime-sized buffers, packed projections, and separate KV page mappings and attention lengths per sequence. Request count does not enlarge the KV pool.
- Static batching and a continuous scheduler that admit queued prompts according to available page budgets, then return their pages and budgets on completion.
- Direct paged decode attention with FP32 online softmax. Each query head streams its sequence's cached pages and accumulates weighted values without gathering a contiguous prefix or storing attention scores.
Part 8 explains Prefill, Decode, and the KV Cache. Part 9 follows with Static and Continuous Batching, including the current paged cache and online-softmax decode attention.
The Llama 3.2 1B inference path includes dense causal prefill, paged decode attention, and static or continuous batching. Model dimensions and the 2,048-token context remain fixed for this learning engine. The KV pool defaults to 128 MiB and can be set with --kv-cache-mib N; active request capacity follows the workload's page budgets rather than a fixed two-request limit.
Admission guarantees room for each request's maximum processed prefix: prompt_tokens + allowed_new_tokens - 1, rounded up to 16-token pages in each of the 16 layers. The allowed output budget is clamped to the context limit, and the final predicted token is returned without being processed again. These admission credits are separate from physical pages, which are assigned lazily. Early completion releases both the assigned pages and the remaining credits.
Requests wait in FIFO order when their budgets cannot fit alongside active requests. Active requests have room to finish, so future page-boundary growth cannot exhaust the pool or deadlock generation. A request whose budget exceeds the entire pool is rejected with a clear error. This conservative policy avoids preemption and recomputation; a large requested output budget can limit concurrency even if the model eventually stops early.
--stats reports the pool size, peak active requests, largest decode batch, peak assigned pages, admission waits, and final free-page count. Prefill still processes one prompt at a time between decode iterations.
BF16 computations can round differently at different batch sizes. When vocabulary logits are nearly tied, greedy output tokens can therefore differ between individual and batched runs. Bitwise output equality across batch sizes is not guaranteed.
- A CUDA-capable NVIDIA GPU and CUDA Toolkit
- CMake 3.24+
- A C++17 compiler
- ICU development libraries
- The nlohmann/json header
- Model weights at models/llama-3.2-1b-instruct/model.safetensors
- The matching tokenizer at models/llama-3.2-1b-instruct/tokenizer.model (copy it from models/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct/original/tokenizer.model)
mkdir -p models/llama-3.2-1b-instruct
cp models/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct/original/tokenizer.model models/llama-3.2-1b-instruct/
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build -j
./build/samir-vllm "Explain the KV cache in two sentences." 128
# Continuous batching (default): admit requests whose page budgets fit.
./build/samir-vllm "Say hello." 64 "Explain the KV cache." "What is RoPE?"
# Static batching: wait for the current group before admitting more.
./build/samir-vllm --static "Say hello." 64 "Explain the KV cache." "What is RoPE?"
# More than two requests share the same default 128 MiB pool.
./build/samir-vllm --stats "Explain paging." 64 "Explain GQA." "Explain RoPE." "Explain softmax."
# A smaller pool queues requests when their declared budgets cannot fit together.
./build/samir-vllm --kv-cache-mib 8 --stats "Explain paging." 64 "Explain GQA." "Explain RoPE."
./build/tokenizer-test models/llama-3.2-1b-instruct/tokenizer.model
After optional --static, --continuous, --kv-cache-mib N, and --stats flags, the first argument is a prompt and the second is max_new_tokens (default: 128). Any remaining arguments are additional prompts; the token budget applies to each request. Every prompt is formatted as an Instruct user message. Generation stops independently at EOS, EOT, or EOM, or the output/context limit, and each completed response is printed with its token IDs and request number.
Prompts are prefilled one at a time, pausing decode. Each decode step packs one token from every active sequence into the shared buffers. Attention reads only that sequence's cache; requests can have different prompt and output lengths. Continuous batching admits waiting requests when page credits become available, while static batching admits the next group after the current group finishes.
src/           Engine entry point, CUDA kernels, and tokenizer implementation
include/       Public kernel and tokenizer headers
tests/         Tokenizer tests
python/        Tokenizer reference script
proper_notes/  Study-notes index, markdown/ sources, and pdf/ reading editions
scripts/       Rebuild the study-note PDFs
notes.md       Working notes from the build
The engine source code in src/, include/, tests/, and python/, along with CMakeLists.txt, .gitignore, and this README, is licensed under the MIT License.
The notes in proper_notes/, notes.md, and podLibraryInstall.md, along with handwritten notes, scans, illustrations, photographs of notes, and PDFs provided with this project, are all rights reserved and excluded from MIT. Personal reading and study are permitted. Redistribution, republication, rehosting, resale, or distribution of adapted versions requires prior written permission, whether offered for free or for payment. See LICENSE-NOTES for the full terms and exceptions.
Public repositories can still be viewed and forked within GitHub under GitHub's Terms of Service.
Built with Llama. The bundled Llama 3.2 tokenizer and any separately downloaded Llama 3.2 weights retain Meta's Llama 3.2 Community License and Acceptable Use Policy. They are excluded from MIT. Keep the agreement, policy, and attribution notice with any redistributed Llama materials.
Third-party dependencies, including CUDA, cuBLAS, ICU, and nlohmann/json, retain their respective licenses.

These admission credits are separate from physical pages, which are assigned lazily. Early completion releases both the assigned pages and the remaining credits.
Requests wait in FIFO order when their budgets cannot fit alongside active requests. Active requests have room to finish, so future page-boundary growth cannot exhaust the pool or deadlock generation. A request whose budget exceeds the entire pool is rejected with a clear error. This conservative policy avoids preemption and recomputation; a large requested output budget can limit concurrency even if the model eventually stops early.
--stats reports the pool size, peak active requests, largest decode batch, peak assigned pages, admission waits, and final free-page count. Prefill still processes one prompt at a time between decode iterations.
BF16 computations can round differently at different batch sizes. When vocabulary logits are nearly tied, greedy output tokens can therefore differ between individual and batched runs. Bitwise output equality across batch sizes is not guaranteed.
- A CUDA-capable NVIDIA GPU and CUDA Toolkit
- CMake 3.24+
- A C++17 compiler
- ICU development libraries
- The nlohmann/json header
- Model weights at models/llama-3.2-1b-instruct/model.safetensors
- The matching tokenizer at models/llama-3.2-1b-instruct/tokenizer.model (copy it from models/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct/original/tokenizer.model)
mkdir -p models/llama-3.2-1b-instruct
cp models/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct/original/tokenizer.model models/llama-3.2-1b-instruct/
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build -j
./build/samir-vllm "Explain the KV cache in two sentences." 128
# Continuous batching (default): admit requests whose page budgets fit.
./build/samir-vllm "Say hello." 64 "Explain the KV cache." "What is RoPE?"
# Static batching: wait for the current group before admitting more.
./build/samir-vllm --static "Say hello." 64 "Explain the KV cache." "What is RoPE?"
# More than two requests share the same default 128 MiB pool.
./build/samir-vllm --stats "Explain paging." 64 "Explain GQA." "Explain RoPE." "Explain softmax."
# A smaller pool queues requests when their declared budgets cannot fit together.
./build/samir-vllm --kv-cache-mib 8 --stats "Explain paging." 64 "Explain GQA." "Explain RoPE."
./build/tokenizer-test models/llama-3.2-1b-instruct/tokenizer.model
After optional --static, --continuous, --kv-cache-mib N, and --stats flags, the first argument is a prompt and the second is max_new_tokens (default: 128). Any remaining arguments are additional prompts; the token budget applies to each request. Every prompt is formatted as an Instruct user message. Generation stops independently at EOS, EOT, or EOM, or the output/context limit, and each completed response is printed with its token IDs and request number.
Prompts are prefilled one at a time, pausing decode. Each decode step packs one token from every active sequence into the shared buffers. Attention reads only that sequence's cache; requests can have different prompt and output lengths. Continuous batching admits waiting requests when page credits become available, while static batching admits the next group after the current group finishes.

tests/         Tokenizer tests
