articles.title: Exact – a new cross platform UI framework by the Expo team
articles.body:
Write an app once. It runs natively on the web, macOS, iOS, and Linux, and an AI agent can build it, run it, see it, and test it on every one of them. Tip Try it with a coding agent. On a Mac with Xcode, Rust, Bun, and Chrome installed, give Claude Code this prompt: Clone https://github.com/expo/exact and follow its README to make a new Exact app with `exact new`. Run `bun scripts/exact.mjs setup` once first. Make a todo list where I can add items, check them off, delete them, and see how many are left. Put the view in Contract and keep the list in `app.ts`. Write an `app.test.contract`, pass it on web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator with `scripts/agent.mjs`, then open the app for me on all three. A fresh agent given an earlier version of this prompt on a clean clone (Hermes already in the machine cache, Cargo's cache warm) finished in about 57 minutes, and its tests passed on all three platforms. About 25 of those minutes were the first macOS and iOS builds, roughly 13 minutes each; later builds take a minute or two. On a machine that has lacked Hermes, its source build came first and added time. Current setup downloads and verifies the pinned host/iOS bundles once instead; ordinary builds stay offline. One app.contract, the same screen on three hosts, captured by the agent driver. Softwear is a demonstration store you can generate from exact-templates: it shows Alternative Apparel's catalog, is not affiliated with that brand, and takes no real orders or payments. Exact is a cross-platform application runtime. You describe your interface in Contract, a small declarative language, and you write your data logic in TypeScript or Rust. The Contract compiler turns the interface into a compact plan. On the web, that plan becomes one ES module over a ~20 KB runtime that drives the real DOM. On macOS, iOS, and Linux, a Rust runner executes the same plan, a Rust layout kernel computes every box with CSS rules, and each platform draws with its own tools: AppKit, UIKit, or a GPU painter. There is no webview and no JavaScript bridge in the UI, and no app JavaScript runs before the first pixel. Note Exact is pre-1.0 and changes daily. There is no API stability, no backwards compatibility, and no migration guide, by design. Upgrade note: Snapback mutation replies with ok: false now throw refused(why) and expose failure(slot); the snapback4 package's README has the before/after and inherited-app commands. Exact assumes much of the code will be written by AI agents. An agent can make an app, run it, look at it, operate it, and prove it works without a person in the loop. - Ten operations, the same on every host. tree · screenshot · tap · type · state · layout · logs · clock · prefer · perf drive the web, macOS, iOS (Simulator or a real iPhone), and Linux through one script, scripts/agent.mjs. There are ten on purpose: an agent API grows one reasonable addition at a time until no one can hold it in mind. - The clock belongs to the agent. Between two operations nothing moves. Instead of sleeping until an animation finishes, the agent says clock +60000 or clock settle and reads the result. No timing flakes, no waits. - Tests are scripts of those operations. An app.test.contract file runs unchanged on any host, with no second evaluator. - Every tool speaks to machines. contract build --json gives diagnostics with stable ids and source ranges. contract symbols gives navigation. A development source map leads from any node on screen back to the line that declared it. The driver refuses to drive a build older than its sources and names the rebuild. - Contract is small on purpose. A whole app fits in a context window. Every write is declared, every list is keyed, every value is typed. Mistakes are refusals that say what to do, not quiet misbehavior. bun scripts/agent.mjs web tree "tap change-station" "type station-search Palo" \ "clock +60000" state "screenshot out.png" Speed of the app and speed of the loop. Each budget in rules/RULES.md is tracked on every commit, and a regression is a P0 with a name on it. How the design keeps those numbers: - The boot path executes and compiles nothing. TypeScript is compiled to Hermes bytecode at build time and loads after the first pixel. The first frame comes from data baked into the plan. - Pay only for what you use. GPU rendering, the Markdown editor, text flow, and browser SQLite are separate artifacts, loaded on demand. Nothing is a feature flag on a core crate. - The web gets its own small runtime. On the RealWorld ("Conduit") benchmark, Exact's runtime was up about 300 ms before the React SSR build had hydrated. It used 26 KB of code against React's 81 KB (the RealWorld benchmark in apps/realworld). - Edits land in about a tenth of a second. On a fresh app made by exact new, a saved Contract or TypeScript edit was rebuilt and in the page in 99 ms. What you write is CSS: the vocabulary, the layout model, the development loop. What you leave unsaid is the platform's: controls, colour, type, motion, gestures, the keyboard and accessibility come out as an app built by hand with UIKit or AppKit would have them, and on the web as a carefully built web app would. What you write wins. The order is author, then platform, then CSS's default, and one test settles a dispute: would someone who knows the platform notice? - Layout is CSS's, because a person can't see a layout default, only its result. A bare node is display: block, box-sizing: content-box, flex-direction: row, flex-shrink: 1, the same as a bare
. - Names are CSS's, because names are what you write: font-size, object-fit, text-overflow, line-clamp, light-dark(), env(safe-area-inset-top). The compiler refuses an alias and names the web's spelling. - Unsaid presentation is the platform's. Text is the system's label colour and size (17 points on an iPhone, 13 on a Mac, the reader's setting in a browser), a button is the system's button, a pushed screen has the system's Back. An app that says less looks more at home. - The browser is the parity oracle for layout and for what you wrote. Native layout given the same inputs, Canvas 2D, SVG, gradients, and authored motion are checked against what Chrome draws. - The web is also the development loop. You work on the seconds-long web loop, and the native hosts are swept behind you. - Any unavoidable deviation in layout is declared, with its reason. For example, Taffy has no position: static. Writing the web doesn't mean the lowest common denominator. Where a platform can do more (real HTML in an SVG foreignObject on the web, MapKit through a native module on Apple), Exact lets it. flowchart LR subgraph author["You write"] C["app.contract
view · state · actions"] D["app.ts or a Rust crate
data sources"] end C --> K["Contract compiler"] --> P["plan
tables + bytecode"] P --> W["Web
one ES module, ~20 KB runtime,
the browser's DOM and CSS"] P --> R["Rust runner
+ layout kernel (Taffy)"] R --> M["macOS
AppKit + CoreText"] R --> I["iOS
UIKit + CoreText"] R --> L["Linux
vello GPU / tiny-skia CPU"] D -.->|answers, checked against declared shapes| W D -.-> R - Contract (contract/) is compiled in four passes: syntax, types, analysis, and lowering. At build time the plan is baked: constant data is evaluated into it, so the first frame needs nothing else. - The runner (runner/) is the plan's virtual machine. It handles keyed component instances, events, timers on a seekable clock, and the data seam. - The kernel (kernel/) is a columnar node arena with CSS layout through a patched Taffy. The host measures text: CoreText on Apple, cosmic-text on Linux. On the web, the browser lays out the same CSS itself, so the web build carries no layout engine. - Hosts (host/) present the tree. The web host writes DOM nodes, and the browser runs CSS transitions. The Apple host is a static library with a C ABI under AppKit and UIKit presenters. The Linux host paints the tree itself, onto DRM/KMS with evdev input, or into an offscreen buffer. - Data sources sit below one seam. TypeScript runs on Hermes on native hosts and in the browser's own engine on the web. Rust runs natively, and can be replaced live (as a shared library, or as Wasm on iOS and the web). Every answer is checked against the shape Contract declared. Grants control network, files, SQLite, and secrets. - Optional pieces are separate artifacts: a wgpu GPU module (Metal on Apple, WebGPU in the browser), native modules (a hyphenated tag backed by a platform widget, like MapKit), and a game engine add-on. These steps were run on macOS on Apple Silicon. Linux works for the web loop and the Linux host. - Rust through rustup. The pinned stable toolchain in rust-toolchain.toml installs itself the first time Cargo runs. - Bun 1.4.2, the version package.json pins. Node and npm are not needed. - Google Chrome. The agent drives the web through headless Chrome. Set CHROME to use another Chromium. - Xcode, for the macOS and iOS hosts. - Hermes, only for TypeScript apps on native hosts. Exact consumes Ibex's pinned, attested 260318099.0.4 release bundle; ordinary Cargo builds are offline and never download or compile an engine. Install it once for each target before building (for this Mac, use aarch64-apple-darwin): cargo run --manifest-path vendor/ibex/crates/hermes-lean-sys-installer/Cargo.toml -- --target The installer verifies the bundle and publishes it under ~/.cargo/hermes-lean-sys/. The v4 set supports macOS, Linux, Windows, iOS devices and the universal iOS Simulator, plus tvOS devices and arm64 tvOS Simulators. Linux and Windows select Ibex's English intl tier; Apple keeps Hermes's OS-backed Intl. HERMES_LEAN_SYS_DIR is only an explicit development override, not normal setup. To install the pinned Bun beside any existing installation: curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | BUN_INSTALL=~/.bun-1.4.2 bash -s bun-v1.4.2. Use ~/.bun-1.4.2/bin/bun for the commands below if it is not on your PATH. bun scripts/exact.mjs setup installs the declared stable and web nightly Rust toolchains, their components/targets (the nightly's clippy lints a game's web bake), matching wasm-bindgen, pinned Binaryen and Bun dependencies, installs the pinned Hermes host bundle and the iOS/tvOS bundles this Mac builds, and fetches the crates of exact2's lock and the game SDK's (game/app/shells.lock), since every bake resolves offline. It keeps Binaryen in ~/.cache/exact/binaryen; builds find it automatically. setup --check invokes Ibex's installer in its offline check mode for that same target set. The resolver authenticates the canonical receipts, archives, compiler and host/target HBC pairing without installing anything; its exit status and diagnostic are the check's result. git clone https://github.com/expo/exact.git cd exact bun scripts/exact.mjs setup bun host/web/dev.mjs # Caltrain, at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ The first run compiles the toolchain, which takes a few minutes. After that, open apps/caltrain/app.contract, change some text, and save. The page rebuilds and reloads in about a tenth of a second. Add --lan to open the same page from a phone on your network. The server answers only to the names it prints (a DNS-rebinding guard; any other Host gets 421); to share it through a tunnel, name the tunnel's host with --allow-host (repeatable; name:port pins a port). An allowed name reaches the page and its reload stream, never the local installer's token. bun host/apple/build.mjs --run # macOS bun host/apple/build.mjs --ios --run # an iOS Simulator (--device --run for a connected iPhone) cargo build --profile host-dev -p caltrain-linux # Linux: a DRM/KMS console, or headless anywhere (--release to ship) A first native build takes ten to fifteen minutes on a laptop; later builds reuse it and take a minute or two. Watch its output rather than waiting blind. iOS commands use an iPhone simulator that's already booted, or boot the newest iPhone Pro. To choose one, set EXACT_SIM to its name or UDID (or pass --sim to build.mjs), and keep the same setting for agent.mjs ios. On Linux, a development build can serve its screen with EXACT_VNC=1 and EXACT_VNC_PASSWORD set to 1–8 bytes. It listens on 127.0.0.1:5900; an explicit EXACT_VNC=host:port selects another address. Production bakes ignore both variables. bun host/web/build.mjs caltrain-web # the build the agent's web host serves bun scripts/agent.mjs web tree "tap change-station" "type station-search Palo" state "screenshot out.png" bun scripts/agent.mjs web --test apps/caltrain/app.test.contract Swap web for macos, ios, or linux once that host is built. Caltrain's three tests take about two seconds on the web host. Each operation is one shell argument, so quote it: "type new-todo Buy milk" types Buy milk (everything after the target is the text). "screenshot film.png over 600 every 50" films motion as a contact sheet; use an .apng name to get an animation. bun scripts/exact.mjs new ../hello # or run `bun link` once, then `exact new ../hello` cd ../hello bun exact.mjs contract types app.contract -o app.contract.d.ts # first run builds the compiler bun exact.mjs web # the dev loop, at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ bun exact.mjs test web tests/*.test.contract # the app's *.test.contract, or the files named bun exact.mjs mac --run # this Mac bun exact.mjs ios --run # an iOS Simulator exact new creates a standalone app: app.contract (the view), app.ts (its data), app.json (the manifest: name, bundle id, hosts, deploy policy), and small web/ and apple/ host crates. Its AGENTS.md (and CLAUDE.md) points a coding agent at docs/start-here.md, the one guide it must read, and at bun exact.mjs help for the commands, including bun exact.mjs contract … for the compiler and contract vocab for the card of what an app writes (--all: every tag and property Contract accepts). Before any of it, run bun scripts/exact.mjs setup once; setup --check names everything this machine is missing without changing it. It has its own Cargo workspace, which uses your exact2 checkout by path. To drive it from exact2, point EXACT_APP_DIR at it: EXACT_APP_DIR=../hello bun host/web/build.mjs hello-web EXACT_APP_DIR=../hello bun scripts/agent.mjs web --app hello tree "screenshot hello.png" Look at every screenshot, not just the test result: a test passes on a layout that spills off the screen. bun exact.mjs agent "screenshot out.png" shows the app on each host in its own session; for a copy you launched yourself, use xcrun simctl io screenshot out.png on iOS. bun scripts/exact.mjs also runs apps from this repository as real Mac apps: exact run markdown README.md, or exact install markdown to put mdview on your PATH. exact list shows what's here. An app's AGENTS.md asks its agent to record friction in one line, bun exact.mjs feedback note "". A failed or slow drive, build or verify, and a passing test or verify, end with one line naming it, at most once a day per project. A note stays in the app's .exact/ with exact2's commit, the last command's verb, exit code and duration, and the OS; never any command output, or the app's code or files. It goes to Expo (https://exact-diaries.ccheever-0f6.workers.dev) only when the project's answer allows: always, or a yes to ask, the default, after bun exact.mjs feedback shows exactly what would go. bun exact.mjs feedback never stops it for a project; EXACT_FEEDBACK=0 silences the nudges and refuses every send on the machine. docs/diary.md has the details. An agent building an app starts at start-here.md, the only required reading, then looks up the recipe for each question. For more, read the complete guide for humans, or look things up in the guide for agents or the grammar and vocabulary reference. Contract describes what an app shows and how its state changes. It doesn't fetch, read files, or run arbitrary code. That's what data sources are for. Here is a complete todo app: a Contract file, a TypeScript file, and a test. This exact app was built for web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator, and its test passed on all three. To try it in an app created with exact new, replace app.contract and app.test.contract with the examples below. In app.ts, keep the generated export const appId = … line and replace the rest with the TypeScript below. // app.contract: the view, its state, and what each action changes. It names no colour, // font or control size: each host draws its own heading, field, button, checkbox and list. shape Todo id: string title: string done: bool shape Change count: number component Todos state draft = "" mutation changed as shape Change refreshes todos resource todos = todos() as shape Todo[] derive left = todos.filter(t => not t.done).length action edit(value: string) draft = value action add if draft.trim() != "" send changed = addTodo(draft.trim()) draft = "" action toggle(id: string, done: bool) send changed = setDone(id, done) action remove(id: string) send changed = removeTodo(id) view list appearance="auto" height="100%" section header text `${left} left` role="heading" testId="count" row input value=draft input=edit submit=add placeholder="What needs doing?" aria-label="New todo" testId="new-todo" flex=1 min-width=0 button press=add buttonStyle="filled" testId="add" text "Add" section for t in todos key=t.id row testId=`todo-${t.id}` input type="checkbox" checked=t.done change=toggle(t.id) aria-label=t.title testId=`toggle-${t.id}` text t.title flex=1 button press=remove(t.id) destructive=true testId=`remove-${t.id}` text "Delete" // app.ts: keeps the list, and answers what app.contract asks for import type { Answer, Sources } from './app.contract.d.ts'; export const grants = ''; // e.g. 'net.fetch https://api.example.com' type Todo = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean }; let todos: Todo[] = []; let next = 1; const sources: Sources = { todos: () => todos, addTodo: ([title]) => { todos = [...todos, { id: String(next++), title, done: false }]; return { count: todos.length }; }, setDone: ([id, done]) => { todos = todos.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done } : t)); return { count: todos.length }; }, removeTodo: ([id]) => { todos = todos.filter((t) => t.id !== id); return { count: todos.length }; }, }; export const answer: Answer = (source, args, store, storage, native) => sources[source](args, store, storage, native);// app.test.contract: runs on any host with `scripts/agent.mjs --test` test "add, finish and delete" expect text "count" == "0 left" type "new-todo" "Buy milk" tap "add" type "new-todo" "Walk the dog" type "new-todo" key "Enter" expect text "count" == "2 left" tap "toggle-1" expect text "count" == "1 left" tap "remove-1" expect tree missing "todo-1" expect tree has "todo-2" The view never edits the list itself. An action sends a mutation to a source, app.ts changes its data and answers, and refreshes todos asks for the list again. Data lives in one place, and every change to it is a named, typed call an agent can see. This list lives in memory. To keep it across launches, give app.ts a grant like sqlite.open app:/data/todos.db and use storage.sqlite, as Fieldnotes does. - No JavaScript in the view, and no I/O. Expressions have no effects. Effects happen only in actions, as assignments, send, refresh, or commands like focus(…) and share(…). Data crosses one seam: a source answers, and the runner checks the answer. - No loops in actions, no await. A list is a view's keyed for, a computation is a derive or a fn (an action may name a value with let), and anything slower lives in a source. A list that changes changes where its data lives, through a mutation, as in the example above. That's what lets the plan be baked, diffed, inspected, and executed the same way on four hosts. - No escape hatch; access hatches. Nothing steps outside the plan. Where an app needs a platform widget, it uses a native module: a hyphenated tag like exact-map, backed by Swift, Kotlin or Rust, laid out by the kernel like any other box. Where it needs the platform object Exact itself built (a UIView, a navigation controller, a DOM element), it marks the node hatch="word" and its native code is handed that object: an access hatch, the panel a machine is built with so its insides can be reached. It configures what Exact made and changes Contract state only by acting on authored nodes, as a person would. These limits serve the principles. An agent can't wire up a data race it can't write. A plan with no JavaScript in it starts fast. A view written in CSS's own words lays out the same on every host and looks at home on each. $ cargo run -q -p contract -- build app.contract app.contract:4:5 [type-assign] `count` is `number`, cannot assign `string` app.contract:7:23 [lower-unknown-attr] `text` has no attribute `size`; `size` is spelled `font-size` here, the web's name One run reports up to twenty independent errors, not just the first. Other subcommands: --json for tools, symbols (definitions and references as JSON), fmt (source-preserving), types (generates app.contract.d.ts for TypeScript sources), and rust (shapes for a Rust data crate). The full language is specified in docs/contract-grammar.md. Each app lives in apps//. Run one on the web with bun host/web/dev.mjs --app , on macOS with bun host/apple/build.mjs -apple --run, and on iOS by adding --ios. All of these screenshots come from the web host, taken by scripts/agent.mjs. To learn from, start with Shelf, the recipe app. It names no colour and no font size, and scripts/no-tells.mjs holds it to that, so it shows what an app that leaves presentation to the platform looks like on each host. Then read these four for what each teaches. They were written before Exact left presentation to the platform and paint their own colours and sizes, so take their structure, not their style: The v1 bar: one real application, not a demo, runs from a single Contract source on web, macOS, iOS, and Linux, within the time budgets in rules/RULES.md. Caltrain is that application, and it runs on all four. Everything else here was admitted because a real app needed it. - Four hosts. Web, macOS (AppKit, no SwiftUI), iOS (UIKit, on the Simulator and on devices), and Linux (GPU or CPU painting, DRM/KMS or headless). Existing Swift apps can embed Exact sessions through ExactKit. - Layout and text. CSS block, flex, and grid; position: static and containing blocks; aspect-ratio; declared fonts; text around shapes. - Paint. Gradients, shadows, backdrop-filter, glass materials, complete SVG, Canvas 2D on every host, and a wgpu GPU canvas loaded after first pixel. - Motion. CSS transitions, springs, @keyframes, follow-and-release gestures (pan, swipe, pinch) with release velocity, layout transitions, exit animations, and scroll- or drag-linked timelines. - Lists. Virtualized lists, vertical or horizontal, one level deep. The rows of a vertical list are its platform's: UIKit's separators and highlight, a table on the Mac, one line between rows on the web, with nothing drawn by the app. - Controls and media. Inputs, select, a WYSIWYG Markdown editor on the web, macOS, and iOS, images including animated ones, video, pickers for an app's declared file types, and share. - Data. TypeScript or Rust sources, optionally on a worker. Grant-checked fetch and streams, files and SQLite (native and in the browser), Keychain secrets, and OAuth sign-in. A router keeps a stack per tab. - Native modules. Platform widgets as hyphenated tags. - The web, server side. Pages pre-rendered at build time or per request by a Rust renderer, then adopted in place instead of hydrated. - Delivery. scripts/deploy.mjs publishes the web root and signed update bundles, which installed apps fetch after first pixel. Apple apps check every fifteen minutes while active under every activation policy; deploy.check.interval overrides the interval in seconds. Checks stage a candidate; deploy.activate controls when it applies. TypeScript and Rust logic can be replaced live in development. Every web build gets an install page, and exact release signs and notarizes a Mac app. - Agents and tests. The ten operations on every host, including a physical iPhone; Contract tests; source maps; filmed screenshots. - Windows. Apps default to ink on a DirectX 11 composition swap chain, or CPU when the manifest declares game. host.windows.painter: "ink" or "cpu" selects either painter, and EXACT_PAINTER overrides both. Skirmish is a standalone game built with Exact's optional game engine; the CPU default preserves its module-owned window presentation. Windows Desk demonstrates native controls over Contract and the kernel with an app-local Win32 presenter; general Windows control parity and delivery remain unfinished. - Android. Early. An app builds for Android and runs on an emulator or a phone: bun exact.mjs android builds it, bun exact.mjs test android runs its tests, and bun exact.mjs agent android … drives it. It needs the Android SDK, the Rust target aarch64-linux-android, and the Hermes Android bundle (bun scripts/hermes-android.mjs build) until an Ibex release ships one. Delivery and store packaging don't exist yet. - No JSX or React tier. Nothing runs JavaScript above the data seam. The door stays open, but no one is building it. - TypeScript can't import npm packages' code yet. app.ts imports its own local files; from a package it imports only types (import type), which the build checks and never runs. - Code updates in production. Signed delivery covers plans and assets. Signed delivery of TypeScript or Rust modules isn't implemented, and app-store rules limit it anyway. - Linux editing. The web and Apple hosts edit; Linux reads. Linux also has no word segmenter, so flowed Thai, Lao, Khmer, and Myanmar text breaks only at spaces. - Out on purpose for v1. Camera access, a gesture arena, general layout animation, grid or masonry virtualization, a general webview beyond iframe, and a devtools UI. - No packaged CLI. You work from a source checkout. exact new apps refer to it by path. Start with rules/RULES.md, one page on how work happens here. Agents should also read AGENTS.md. In short: - Six blocking checks, 65 seconds in total. Anything slower runs asynchronously, per commit. cargo build --all-targets --keep-going cargo test --tests --no-fail-fast cargo clippy --all-targets --keep-going -- -D warnings && cargo fmt --all -- --check bun scripts/caps.mjs # budgets: 1,500 lines per source file, document caps bun scripts/boot.mjs # counts the module graph before first pixel cargo check --workspace --all-targets --keep-going # every crate compiles The first three build and test Cargo's default-members. The last compiles every other crate too, so a host or an app outside them cannot stop compiling unseen. It needs the pinned Bun (package.json) first on PATH: app crates' build scripts run it. - Verify by running, not by reading. Build the app a change touches and drive it: bun scripts/smoke.mjs drives the whole app on that host. - Delete; don't deprecate. Before 1.0 there are no compatibility shims. Generated files are built, never committed. - Agents remove apparatus freely and add none (checks, scripts, registries, design documents) without a person saying so. - A spec gets written only when it has an implementer and a date. Detailed operational notes cover toolchains, the Contract CLI's JSON formats, source maps, TypeScript and Rust data modules, storage, live replacement, delivery trust, the install page, and the stress harnesses. They're in docs/reference.md. The workspace is MIT-licensed (Cargo.toml). Exact’s Snapback4 adapter uses published 0.4.33 with the matching immutable Rust source revision 3653cae823145170df3e720f5e321bd1b5b4d79d. See the snapback4 package's README for wiring and device rebuilds.

articles.title: Exact – a new cross platform UI framework
articles.body:
Write an app once. It runs natively on the web, macOS, iOS, and Linux, and an AI agent can build it, run it, see it, and test it on every one of them. Tip Try it with a coding agent. On a Mac with Xcode, Rust, Bun, and Chrome installed, give Claude Code this prompt: Clone https://github.com/expo/exact and follow its README to make a new Exact app with `exact new`. Run `bun scripts/exact.mjs setup` once first. Make a todo list where I can add items, check them off, delete them, and see how many are left. Put the view in Contract and keep the list in `app.ts`. Write an `app.test.contract`, pass it on web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator with `scripts/agent.mjs`, then open the app for me on all three. A fresh agent given an earlier version of this prompt on a clean clone (Hermes already in the machine cache, Cargo's cache warm) finished in about 57 minutes, and its tests passed on all three platforms. About 25 of those minutes were the first macOS and iOS builds, roughly 13 minutes each; later builds take a minute or two. On a machine that has lacked Hermes, its source build came first and added time. Current setup downloads and verifies the pinned host/iOS bundles once instead; ordinary builds stay offline. One app.contract, the same screen on three hosts, captured by the agent driver. Softwear is a demonstration store you can generate from exact-templates: it shows Alternative Apparel's catalog, is not affiliated with that brand, and takes no real orders or payments. Exact is a cross-platform application runtime. You describe your interface in Contract, a small declarative language, and you write your data logic in TypeScript or Rust. The Contract compiler turns the interface into a compact plan. On the web, that plan becomes one ES module over a ~20 KB runtime that drives the real DOM. On macOS, iOS, and Linux, a Rust runner executes the same plan, a Rust layout kernel computes every box with CSS rules, and each platform draws with its own tools: AppKit, UIKit, or a GPU painter. There is no webview and no JavaScript bridge in the UI, and no app JavaScript runs before the first pixel. Note Exact is pre-1.0 and changes daily. There is no API stability, no backwards compatibility, and no migration guide, by design. Upgrade note: Snapback mutation replies with ok: false now throw refused(why) and expose failure(slot); the snapback4 package's README has the before/after and inherited-app commands. Exact assumes much of the code will be written by AI agents. An agent can make an app, run it, look at it, operate it, and prove it works without a person in the loop. - Ten operations, the same on every host. tree · screenshot · tap · type · state · layout · logs · clock · prefer · perf drive the web, macOS, iOS (Simulator or a real iPhone), and Linux through one script, scripts/agent.mjs. There are ten on purpose: an agent API grows one reasonable addition at a time until no one can hold it in mind. - The clock belongs to the agent. Between two operations nothing moves. Instead of sleeping until an animation finishes, the agent says clock +60000 or clock settle and reads the result. No timing flakes, no waits. - Tests are scripts of those operations. An app.test.contract file runs unchanged on any host, with no second evaluator. - Every tool speaks to machines. contract build --json gives diagnostics with stable ids and source ranges. contract symbols gives navigation. A development source map leads from any node on screen back to the line that declared it. The driver refuses to drive a build older than its sources and names the rebuild. - Contract is small on purpose. A whole app fits in a context window. Every write is declared, every list is keyed, every value is typed. Mistakes are refusals that say what to do, not quiet misbehavior. bun scripts/agent.mjs web tree "tap change-station" "type station-search Palo" \ "clock +60000" state "screenshot out.png" Speed of the app and speed of the loop. Each budget in rules/RULES.md is tracked on every commit, and a regression is a P0 with a name on it. How the design keeps those numbers: - The boot path executes and compiles nothing. TypeScript is compiled to Hermes bytecode at build time and loads after the first pixel. The first frame comes from data baked into the plan. - Pay only for what you use. GPU rendering, the Markdown editor, text flow, and browser SQLite are separate artifacts, loaded on demand. Nothing is a feature flag on a core crate. - The web gets its own small runtime. On the RealWorld ("Conduit") benchmark, Exact's runtime was up about 300 ms before the React SSR build had hydrated. It used 26 KB of code against React's 81 KB (the RealWorld benchmark in apps/realworld). - Edits land in about a tenth of a second. On a fresh app made by exact new, a saved Contract or TypeScript edit was rebuilt and in the page in 99 ms. What you write is CSS: the vocabulary, the layout model, the development loop. What you leave unsaid is the platform's: controls, colour, type, motion, gestures, the keyboard and accessibility come out as an app built by hand with UIKit or AppKit would have them, and on the web as a carefully built web app would. What you write wins. The order is author, then platform, then CSS's default, and one test settles a dispute: would someone who knows the platform notice? - Layout is CSS's, because a person can't see a layout default, only its result. A bare node is display: block, box-sizing: content-box, flex-direction: row, flex-shrink: 1, the same as a bare
. - Names are CSS's, because names are what you write: font-size, object-fit, text-overflow, line-clamp, light-dark(), env(safe-area-inset-top). The compiler refuses an alias and names the web's spelling. - Unsaid presentation is the platform's. Text is the system's label colour and size (17 points on an iPhone, 13 on a Mac, the reader's setting in a browser), a button is the system's button, a pushed screen has the system's Back. An app that says less looks more at home. - The browser is the parity oracle for layout and for what you wrote. Native layout given the same inputs, Canvas 2D, SVG, gradients, and authored motion are checked against what Chrome draws. - The web is also the development loop. You work on the seconds-long web loop, and the native hosts are swept behind you. - Any unavoidable deviation in layout is declared, with its reason. For example, Taffy has no position: static. Writing the web doesn't mean the lowest common denominator. Where a platform can do more (real HTML in an SVG foreignObject on the web, MapKit through a native module on Apple), Exact lets it. flowchart LR subgraph author["You write"] C["app.contract
view · state · actions"] D["app.ts or a Rust crate
data sources"] end C --> K["Contract compiler"] --> P["plan
tables + bytecode"] P --> W["Web
one ES module, ~20 KB runtime,
the browser's DOM and CSS"] P --> R["Rust runner
+ layout kernel (Taffy)"] R --> M["macOS
AppKit + CoreText"] R --> I["iOS
UIKit + CoreText"] R --> L["Linux
vello GPU / tiny-skia CPU"] D -.->|answers, checked against declared shapes| W D -.-> R - Contract (contract/) is compiled in four passes: syntax, types, analysis, and lowering. At build time the plan is baked: constant data is evaluated into it, so the first frame needs nothing else. - The runner (runner/) is the plan's virtual machine. It handles keyed component instances, events, timers on a seekable clock, and the data seam. - The kernel (kernel/) is a columnar node arena with CSS layout through a patched Taffy. The host measures text: CoreText on Apple, cosmic-text on Linux. On the web, the browser lays out the same CSS itself, so the web build carries no layout engine. - Hosts (host/) present the tree. The web host writes DOM nodes, and the browser runs CSS transitions. The Apple host is a static library with a C ABI under AppKit and UIKit presenters. The Linux host paints the tree itself, onto DRM/KMS with evdev input, or into an offscreen buffer. - Data sources sit below one seam. TypeScript runs on Hermes on native hosts and in the browser's own engine on the web. Rust runs natively, and can be replaced live (as a shared library, or as Wasm on iOS and the web). Every answer is checked against the shape Contract declared. Grants control network, files, SQLite, and secrets. - Optional pieces are separate artifacts: a wgpu GPU module (Metal on Apple, WebGPU in the browser), native modules (a hyphenated tag backed by a platform widget, like MapKit), and a game engine add-on. These steps were run on macOS on Apple Silicon. Linux works for the web loop and the Linux host. - Rust through rustup. The pinned stable toolchain in rust-toolchain.toml installs itself the first time Cargo runs. - Bun 1.4.2, the version package.json pins. Node and npm are not needed. - Google Chrome. The agent drives the web through headless Chrome. Set CHROME to use another Chromium. - Xcode, for the macOS and iOS hosts. - Hermes, only for TypeScript apps on native hosts. Exact consumes Ibex's pinned, attested 260318099.0.4 release bundle; ordinary Cargo builds are offline and never download or compile an engine. Install it once for each target before building (for this Mac, use aarch64-apple-darwin): cargo run --manifest-path vendor/ibex/crates/hermes-lean-sys-installer/Cargo.toml -- --target The installer verifies the bundle and publishes it under ~/.cargo/hermes-lean-sys/. The v4 set supports macOS, Linux, Windows, iOS devices and the universal iOS Simulator, plus tvOS devices and arm64 tvOS Simulators. Linux and Windows select Ibex's English intl tier; Apple keeps Hermes's OS-backed Intl. HERMES_LEAN_SYS_DIR is only an explicit development override, not normal setup. To install the pinned Bun beside any existing installation: curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | BUN_INSTALL=~/.bun-1.4.2 bash -s bun-v1.4.2. Use ~/.bun-1.4.2/bin/bun for the commands below if it is not on your PATH. bun scripts/exact.mjs setup installs the declared stable and web nightly Rust toolchains, their components/targets (the nightly's clippy lints a game's web bake), matching wasm-bindgen, pinned Binaryen and Bun dependencies, installs the pinned Hermes host bundle and the iOS/tvOS bundles this Mac builds, and fetches the crates of exact2's lock and the game SDK's (game/app/shells.lock), since every bake resolves offline. It keeps Binaryen in ~/.cache/exact/binaryen; builds find it automatically. setup --check invokes Ibex's installer in its offline check mode for that same target set. The resolver authenticates the canonical receipts, archives, compiler and host/target HBC pairing without installing anything; its exit status and diagnostic are the check's result. git clone https://github.com/expo/exact.git cd exact bun scripts/exact.mjs setup bun host/web/dev.mjs # Caltrain, at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ The first run compiles the toolchain, which takes a few minutes. After that, open apps/caltrain/app.contract, change some text, and save. The page rebuilds and reloads in about a tenth of a second. Add --lan to open the same page from a phone on your network. The server answers only to the names it prints (a DNS-rebinding guard; any other Host gets 421); to share it through a tunnel, name the tunnel's host with --allow-host (repeatable; name:port pins a port). An allowed name reaches the page and its reload stream, never the local installer's token. bun host/apple/build.mjs --run # macOS bun host/apple/build.mjs --ios --run # an iOS Simulator (--device --run for a connected iPhone) cargo build --profile host-dev -p caltrain-linux # Linux: a DRM/KMS console, or headless anywhere (--release to ship) A first native build takes ten to fifteen minutes on a laptop; later builds reuse it and take a minute or two. Watch its output rather than waiting blind. iOS commands use an iPhone simulator that's already booted, or boot the newest iPhone Pro. To choose one, set EXACT_SIM to its name or UDID (or pass --sim to build.mjs), and keep the same setting for agent.mjs ios. On Linux, a development build can serve its screen with EXACT_VNC=1 and EXACT_VNC_PASSWORD set to 1–8 bytes. It listens on 127.0.0.1:5900; an explicit EXACT_VNC=host:port selects another address. Production bakes ignore both variables. bun host/web/build.mjs caltrain-web # the build the agent's web host serves bun scripts/agent.mjs web tree "tap change-station" "type station-search Palo" state "screenshot out.png" bun scripts/agent.mjs web --test apps/caltrain/app.test.contract Swap web for macos, ios, or linux once that host is built. Caltrain's three tests take about two seconds on the web host. Each operation is one shell argument, so quote it: "type new-todo Buy milk" types Buy milk (everything after the target is the text). "screenshot film.png over 600 every 50" films motion as a contact sheet; use an .apng name to get an animation. bun scripts/exact.mjs new ../hello # or run `bun link` once, then `exact new ../hello` cd ../hello bun exact.mjs contract types app.contract -o app.contract.d.ts # first run builds the compiler bun exact.mjs web # the dev loop, at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ bun exact.mjs test web tests/*.test.contract # the app's *.test.contract, or the files named bun exact.mjs mac --run # this Mac bun exact.mjs ios --run # an iOS Simulator exact new creates a standalone app: app.contract (the view), app.ts (its data), app.json (the manifest: name, bundle id, hosts, deploy policy), and small web/ and apple/ host crates. Its AGENTS.md (and CLAUDE.md) points a coding agent at docs/start-here.md, the one guide it must read, and at bun exact.mjs help for the commands, including bun exact.mjs contract … for the compiler and contract vocab for the card of what an app writes (--all: every tag and property Contract accepts). Before any of it, run bun scripts/exact.mjs setup once; setup --check names everything this machine is missing without changing it. It has its own Cargo workspace, which uses your exact2 checkout by path. To drive it from exact2, point EXACT_APP_DIR at it: EXACT_APP_DIR=../hello bun host/web/build.mjs hello-web EXACT_APP_DIR=../hello bun scripts/agent.mjs web --app hello tree "screenshot hello.png" Look at every screenshot, not just the test result: a test passes on a layout that spills off the screen. bun exact.mjs agent "screenshot out.png" shows the app on each host in its own session; for a copy you launched yourself, use xcrun simctl io screenshot out.png on iOS. bun scripts/exact.mjs also runs apps from this repository as real Mac apps: exact run markdown README.md, or exact install markdown to put mdview on your PATH. exact list shows what's here. An app's AGENTS.md asks its agent to record friction in one line, bun exact.mjs feedback note "". A failed or slow drive, build or verify, and a passing test or verify, end with one line naming it, at most once a day per project. A note stays in the app's .exact/ with exact2's commit, the last command's verb, exit code and duration, and the OS; never any command output, or the app's code or files. It goes to Expo (https://exact-diaries.ccheever-0f6.workers.dev) only when the project's answer allows: always, or a yes to ask, the default, after bun exact.mjs feedback shows exactly what would go. bun exact.mjs feedback never stops it for a project; EXACT_FEEDBACK=0 silences the nudges and refuses every send on the machine. docs/diary.md has the details. An agent building an app starts at start-here.md, the only required reading, then looks up the recipe for each question. For more, read the complete guide for humans, or look things up in the guide for agents or the grammar and vocabulary reference. Contract describes what an app shows and how its state changes. It doesn't fetch, read files, or run arbitrary code. That's what data sources are for. Here is a complete todo app: a Contract file, a TypeScript file, and a test. This exact app was built for web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator, and its test passed on all three. To try it in an app created with exact new, replace app.contract and app.test.contract with the examples below. In app.ts, keep the generated export const appId = … line and replace the rest with the TypeScript below. // app.contract: the view, its state, and what each action changes. It names no colour, // font or control size: each host draws its own heading, field, button, checkbox and list. shape Todo id: string title: string done: bool shape Change count: number component Todos state draft = "" mutation changed as shape Change refreshes todos resource todos = todos() as shape Todo[] derive left = todos.filter(t => not t.done).length action edit(value: string) draft = value action add if draft.trim() != "" send changed = addTodo(draft.trim()) draft = "" action toggle(id: string, done: bool) send changed = setDone(id, done) action remove(id: string) send changed = removeTodo(id) view list appearance="auto" height="100%" section header text `${left} left` role="heading" testId="count" row input value=draft input=edit submit=add placeholder="What needs doing?" aria-label="New todo" testId="new-todo" flex=1 min-width=0 button press=add buttonStyle="filled" testId="add" text "Add" section for t in todos key=t.id row testId=`todo-${t.id}` input type="checkbox" checked=t.done change=toggle(t.id) aria-label=t.title testId=`toggle-${t.id}` text t.title flex=1 button press=remove(t.id) destructive=true testId=`remove-${t.id}` text "Delete" // app.ts: keeps the list, and answers what app.contract asks for import type { Answer, Sources } from './app.contract.d.ts'; export const grants = ''; // e.g. 'net.fetch https://api.example.com' type Todo = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean }; let todos: Todo[] = []; let next = 1; const sources: Sources = { todos: () => todos, addTodo: ([title]) => { todos = [...todos, { id: String(next++), title, done: false }]; return { count: todos.length }; }, setDone: ([id, done]) => { todos = todos.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done } : t)); return { count: todos.length }; }, removeTodo: ([id]) => { todos = todos.filter((t) => t.id !== id); return { count: todos.length }; }, }; export const answer: Answer = (source, args, store, storage, native) => sources[source](args, store, storage, native);// app.test.contract: runs on any host with `scripts/agent.mjs --test` test "add, finish and delete" expect text "count" == "0 left" type "new-todo" "Buy milk" tap "add" type "new-todo" "Walk the dog" type "new-todo" key "Enter" expect text "count" == "2 left" tap "toggle-1" expect text "count" == "1 left" tap "remove-1" expect tree missing "todo-1" expect tree has "todo-2" The view never edits the list itself. An action sends a mutation to a source, app.ts changes its data and answers, and refreshes todos asks for the list again. Data lives in one place, and every change to it is a named, typed call an agent can see. This list lives in memory. To keep it across launches, give app.ts a grant like sqlite.open app:/data/todos.db and use storage.sqlite, as Fieldnotes does. - No JavaScript in the view, and no I/O. Expressions have no effects. Effects happen only in actions, as assignments, send, refresh, or commands like focus(…) and share(…). Data crosses one seam: a source answers, and the runner checks the answer. - No loops in actions, no await. A list is a view's keyed for, a computation is a derive or a fn (an action may name a value with let), and anything slower lives in a source. A list that changes changes where its data lives, through a mutation, as in the example above. That's what lets the plan be baked, diffed, inspected, and executed the same way on four hosts. - No escape hatch; access hatches. Nothing steps outside the plan. Where an app needs a platform widget, it uses a native module: a hyphenated tag like exact-map, backed by Swift, Kotlin or Rust, laid out by the kernel like any other box. Where it needs the platform object Exact itself built (a UIView, a navigation controller, a DOM element), it marks the node hatch="word" and its native code is handed that object: an access hatch, the panel a machine is built with so its insides can be reached. It configures what Exact made and changes Contract state only by acting on authored nodes, as a person would. These limits serve the principles. An agent can't wire up a data race it can't write. A plan with no JavaScript in it starts fast. A view written in CSS's own words lays out the same on every host and looks at home on each. $ cargo run -q -p contract -- build app.contract app.contract:4:5 [type-assign] `count` is `number`, cannot assign `string` app.contract:7:23 [lower-unknown-attr] `text` has no attribute `size`; `size` is spelled `font-size` here, the web's name One run reports up to twenty independent errors, not just the first. Other subcommands: --json for tools, symbols (definitions and references as JSON), fmt (source-preserving), types (generates app.contract.d.ts for TypeScript sources), and rust (shapes for a Rust data crate). The full language is specified in docs/contract-grammar.md. Each app lives in apps//. Run one on the web with bun host/web/dev.mjs --app , on macOS with bun host/apple/build.mjs -apple --run, and on iOS by adding --ios. All of these screenshots come from the web host, taken by scripts/agent.mjs. To learn from, start with Shelf, the recipe app. It names no colour and no font size, and scripts/no-tells.mjs holds it to that, so it shows what an app that leaves presentation to the platform looks like on each host. Then read these four for what each teaches. They were written before Exact left presentation to the platform and paint their own colours and sizes, so take their structure, not their style: The v1 bar: one real application, not a demo, runs from a single Contract source on web, macOS, iOS, and Linux, within the time budgets in rules/RULES.md. Caltrain is that application, and it runs on all four. Everything else here was admitted because a real app needed it. - Four hosts. Web, macOS (AppKit, no SwiftUI), iOS (UIKit, on the Simulator and on devices), and Linux (GPU or CPU painting, DRM/KMS or headless). Existing Swift apps can embed Exact sessions through ExactKit. - Layout and text. CSS block, flex, and grid; position: static and containing blocks; aspect-ratio; declared fonts; text around shapes. - Paint. Gradients, shadows, backdrop-filter, glass materials, complete SVG, Canvas 2D on every host, and a wgpu GPU canvas loaded after first pixel. - Motion. CSS transitions, springs, @keyframes, follow-and-release gestures (pan, swipe, pinch) with release velocity, layout transitions, exit animations, and scroll- or drag-linked timelines. - Lists. Virtualized lists, vertical or horizontal, one level deep. The rows of a vertical list are its platform's: UIKit's separators and highlight, a table on the Mac, one line between rows on the web, with nothing drawn by the app. - Controls and media. Inputs, select, a WYSIWYG Markdown editor on the web, macOS, and iOS, images including animated ones, video, pickers for an app's declared file types, and share. - Data. TypeScript or Rust sources, optionally on a worker. Grant-checked fetch and streams, files and SQLite (native and in the browser), Keychain secrets, and OAuth sign-in. A router keeps a stack per tab. - Native modules. Platform widgets as hyphenated tags. - The web, server side. Pages pre-rendered at build time or per request by a Rust renderer, then adopted in place instead of hydrated. - Delivery. scripts/deploy.mjs publishes the web root and signed update bundles, which installed apps fetch after first pixel. Apple apps check every fifteen minutes while active under every activation policy; deploy.check.interval overrides the interval in seconds. Checks stage a candidate; deploy.activate controls when it applies. TypeScript and Rust logic can be replaced live in development. Every web build gets an install page, and exact release signs and notarizes a Mac app. - Agents and tests. The ten operations on every host, including a physical iPhone; Contract tests; source maps; filmed screenshots. - Windows. Apps default to ink on a DirectX 11 composition swap chain, or CPU when the manifest declares game. host.windows.painter: "ink" or "cpu" selects either painter, and EXACT_PAINTER overrides both. Skirmish is a standalone game built with Exact's optional game engine; the CPU default preserves its module-owned window presentation. Windows Desk demonstrates native controls over Contract and the kernel with an app-local Win32 presenter; general Windows control parity and delivery remain unfinished. - Android. Early. An app builds for Android and runs on an emulator or a phone: bun exact.mjs android builds it, bun exact.mjs test android runs its tests, and bun exact.mjs agent android … drives it. It needs the Android SDK, the Rust target aarch64-linux-android, and the Hermes Android bundle (bun scripts/hermes-android.mjs build) until an Ibex release ships one. Delivery and store packaging don't exist yet. - No JSX or React tier. Nothing runs JavaScript above the data seam. The door stays open, but no one is building it. - TypeScript can't import npm packages' code yet. app.ts imports its own local files; from a package it imports only types (import type), which the build checks and never runs. - Code updates in production. Signed delivery covers plans and assets. Signed delivery of TypeScript or Rust modules isn't implemented, and app-store rules limit it anyway. - Linux editing. The web and Apple hosts edit; Linux reads. Linux also has no word segmenter, so flowed Thai, Lao, Khmer, and Myanmar text breaks only at spaces. - Out on purpose for v1. Camera access, a gesture arena, general layout animation, grid or masonry virtualization, a general webview beyond iframe, and a devtools UI. - No packaged CLI. You work from a source checkout. exact new apps refer to it by path. Start with rules/RULES.md, one page on how work happens here. Agents should also read AGENTS.md. In short: - Six blocking checks, 65 seconds in total. Anything slower runs asynchronously, per commit. cargo build --all-targets --keep-going cargo test --tests --no-fail-fast cargo clippy --all-targets --keep-going -- -D warnings && cargo fmt --all -- --check bun scripts/caps.mjs # budgets: 1,500 lines per source file, document caps bun scripts/boot.mjs # counts the module graph before first pixel cargo check --workspace --all-targets --keep-going # every crate compiles The first three build and test Cargo's default-members. The last compiles every other crate too, so a host or an app outside them cannot stop compiling unseen. It needs the pinned Bun (package.json) first on PATH: app crates' build scripts run it. - Verify by running, not by reading. Build the app a change touches and drive it: bun scripts/smoke.mjs drives the whole app on that host. - Delete; don't deprecate. Before 1.0 there are no compatibility shims. Generated files are built, never committed. - Agents remove apparatus freely and add none (checks, scripts, registries, design documents) without a person saying so. - A spec gets written only when it has an implementer and a date. Detailed operational notes cover toolchains, the Contract CLI's JSON formats, source maps, TypeScript and Rust data modules, storage, live replacement, delivery trust, the install page, and the stress harnesses. They're in docs/reference.md. The workspace is MIT-licensed (Cargo.toml). Exact’s Snapback4 adapter uses published 0.4.33 with the matching immutable Rust source revision 3653cae823145170df3e720f5e321bd1b5b4d79d. See the snapback4 package's README for wiring and device rebuilds.

articles.title: Show HN: DBDelve – Open-Source DB Client Made with Rust and GPUI
articles.body:
Hi HN, I’m Shayan and a few months ago I started building a DB Client DBDelve with a focus on performance and just making something that feels good to use (in the spirit of Zed, Ghostty, and other tools that just feel pleasant to use).
For my workflow I’ve always looked for performance, especially since some time ago I had a really outdated machine and any kind of bloat was really noticeable, I remember using DBeaver and it just crashing on me multiple times, I also had to use postGIS which just made it worse. I migrated all my essential dev tools to use the ones with performance in mind (Zed, Ghostty etc) but the only thing that was missing was DB Client. The main choices everyone has are DBeaver which is a memory hog and an overkill for most of the tasks imo. The other options like Datagrid, Beekeeper, TablePlus are either electron based so bloated and memory hogs or paid and closed-source.
DBDelve 0.3.6 against DBeaver 25.3.1 on the same Postgres table, median of 5 runs each (2026-10-11, M1 Pro, 32 GB). Times are from the action to the rows rendered.
                            DBDelve   DBeaver
  Launch                    1.1 s     5.2 s
  Idle memory               133 MB    606 MB
  1,000-row query           0.21 s    1.96 s
  1M rows, time             56 s      208 s
  1M rows, memory [1]       4.9 GB    17 GB
[1] The whole 1M-row, 100-column table pulled into memory on purpose, with the row limit off. Not a normal use case; DBeaver's heap limit had to be raised manually for the benchmark.
Scrolling perf with 1 million rows loaded with 100 columns each: https://youtu.be/V2MOhJYFqIE
It has most of the features most devs would need for 90% of their workflow plus some more I thought would be a nice touch:
Readonly, read-write and Full Access modes
Glass themes (If you’re into them, I am)
Keyboard focused with every keybinding customizable
Organization of connections into projects
Me and some other folks have been daily driving it for more than a month now and most good feedback comes on it having a really simple UI to navigate, very stable for its age and the performance of course. I’m also sharing here because those people tell me this has potential to grow so I’m trying my hand at distributing it.
Just want to give a huge shoutout here to the Zed team for GPUI, it's a breeze to work with if you just get through them not updating the crate officially on crates.io but the community has found the solutions for it, you just have to dig deep for it. It performs extremely well and just the HTML-like structure of it, makes it easy to understand for someone from a web dev background and agents are very good at writing it too. GPUI component also solves a lot of problems with having a good component library we can use. I think for anyone starting a GPUI project now, GPUI-kit makes a lot of sense, it just bundles GPUI, GPUI-component together and has some optimizations adding retained mode which is experimental but could provide a lot of benefit, so think all things considered it should be the default way.
The major optimization I did was just lowering the memory overhead by using packed rows which reduced the memory usage by 40% on large datasets (8.1GB to 4.9GB on a 4GB table loaded in app), everything else came bundled in with Rust and GPUI mostly or they just made it very easy.
Limitations:
It's not signed and notarized, identity verification from apple's side has been a nightmare but it should be signed soon.
Don’t expect feature parity with more mature clients for now, the general direction of this right now is the zed way of adding features in but after making sure the core workflows are done with a high quality.
Do give it a try, you can import your connections from dbeaver and tableplus.
https://github.com/ShayanAbbas1/dbdelve

articles.title: E-means: 10x faster k-means at equal loss
articles.body:
I’m excited to open-source e-means: a modern, robust k-means algorithm developed at Meta FAIR. A replacement of Lloyd's algorithm, e-means delivers a ~10× speedup in both epochs and wall-clock time while achieving lower loss.
100,000 datapoints in 200 clusters, two wide Gaussians and three small ones, cut off at a box, on a light uniform background. Lloyd has 1 update against 97 per epoch for e-means.
Across a large range of scales and datasets, e-means reaches a test loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs, in 1.2 to 3 epochs. Measured end to end, that is a 10–45× wall-clock reduction on GPU against the state-of-the-art Lloyd implementation (Flash-KMeans[2]), and 8–15× on CPU against Faiss[1]. Speed and quality usually trade against each other in k-means, while e-means achieves both better speed and loss.
Given a fixed dataset of n points X = {x1, ..., xn} ⊂ Rd and an integer k, the k-means problem is to find k centroids C = (c1, ..., ck) minimizing the mean squared distance between each point and its nearest centroid:
It's a static dataset, unlike codebook learning inside VQ-VAEs, where the distribution to cluster is constantly moving.
The goal of e-means is to provide a modern optimization rule for the k-means problem. We started this project from the following observations:
For e-means, we chose to do mini-batch updates with exponential moving averages[6], which we found to be most efficient for the k-means problem. Contrary to previous mini-batch approaches, e-means requires no hyperparameter tuning because it automatically sets the batch size and step size with scaling laws (see Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws). In addition, e-means improves the initialization and the dead-cluster revival strategy, adds a cosine-scheduled decay rate, and introduces a finalization stage that reduces the training loss for a negligible runtime penalty at the end of training. e-means is highly parallelizable, and comes with specialized kernels that translate its algorithmic advantage into wall-clock speedups.
The centroid update rule is the central component of e-means. This section aims to provide an overview of update rules for k-means clustering. All methods maintain, for each cluster j, a sum Sj and a count Nj of the points assigned to it, and take the centroid as their ratio:
They differ only in how Sj and Nj are updated. Below, sj and nj denote the sum and the count of the points in the current batch that are assigned to cluster j (both zero if none are).
Lloyd’s algorithm[7] assigns every point to its nearest centroid and recomputes the statistics from scratch, using the full dataset as the batch:
so cj is the exact mean of the points currently assigned to it. Each update costs one full pass over the data, and the procedure is repeated a fixed number of times (typically 20 to 50 iterations).
MacQueen’s update[3] accumulates the statistics without ever discarding them:
so cj is the uniform mean of every point assigned to cluster j since the start of training, including points assigned under earlier, possibly poor, centroid positions. This was later partially addressed by Staleness-Reduction Mini-Batch K-Means[8], a hybrid method between k-means and MacQueen. They obtained important speedups, but only on very low numbers of clusters.
e-means works on mini-batches and replaces this sum with an exponential moving average:
so older assignments are forgotten at rate α, and the centroid tracks recent assignments rather than the whole history. This update rule is typically used for moving distributions, hence their adoption for training VQ-VAEs[6]. What we found is that it’s also extremely efficient for static datasets if it’s combined with e-means’ other components, and hyperparameters are properly tuned.
The e-means project started from previous work at Meta FAIR by Hugo Touvron and Hervé Jégou, who had found that mini-batch k-means by gradient descent could beat Lloyd’s algorithm. While I could reproduce these results, I found that the performance of gradient-descent based centroid updates is unstable at large learning rates, unlike exponential moving average updates. I suspect that is because EMA updates guarantee that the centroid is always in the convex hull of points assigned to it, while gradient descent updates may overshoot past that hull.
In order to achieve the lowest loss at a fixed number of epochs, we chose exponential moving average updates, hence the name e-means for our method.
If you set the batch to the full dataset, B = n, and α = 1, then Nj and Sj become exactly the count and sum of the whole cluster, so one e-means iteration becomes exactly one Lloyd iteration. Lloyd is an extreme case of e-means without cosine scheduling on the learning rate. However, our hyperparameter search found that this extreme setting is highly suboptimal, which explains why e-means largely outperforms Lloyd. Below, the loss is measured for every batch size B and step α: Lloyd lands in a corner, well outside the region where the loss is lowest.
This hyperparameter study motivated us to derive scaling laws that automatically pick the optimal batch size B and step size α.
To better understand why e-means reaches better losses than Lloyd at convergence, we plotted a few trainings on toy datasets to evaluate their ability to escape local minima. Repeating trainings over 200 seeds, we found that e-means is much less likely to fall in pathological configurations compared to Lloyd.
Our explanation for that is that mini-batches provide more noisy updates that are more likely to explore the optimization landscape and escape local minima. Lloyd, with its always decreasing loss, is more likely to exploit found local minima and never escape them.
An essential property of e-means is that practitioners don't need to set any additional hyperparameter compared to Lloyd's algorithm. We fitted two scaling laws to set the batch size B and step size α0 from any problem's characteristics (n, k, T), and found them to exhibit strong generalization on unseen datasets and problem scales.
Regret = (MSE with the law − best MSE over the grid) / best MSE, median over configurations. Held-out datasets: SIFT, SPACEV, and the VIBE[9] datasets arXiv and AG-News. Held-out size: one value of n left out of the fit and predicted.
We propose two equations to choose the batch, the default law and the quality law. The “quality law” trades off throughput for better clustering quality against the “default” law. Below we plot the training data for our scaling laws: validation MSE against step size α0 (left) and batch size B (right).
Toy example showing the importance of dead-cluster revival.
The main issue with mini-batch k-means is that it is prone to “dead” clusters, centroids that end up with zero assigned points during optimization. This reduces the effective size of the codebook, which is especially problematic for the large codebooks increasingly used today.
A common mitigation is to reinitialize clusters that fall below a certain size threshold, as done in EnCodec[10], where dead centroids are simply replaced by random samples drawn from the incoming batch. While this helps, it does not fully resolve the issue. Instead of sampling arbitrary points from the batch, we revive dead clusters by splitting large, existing ones: we sample an active cluster with probability proportional to its size and split it into two. We found this approach, adapted from Faiss k-means, to be significantly more effective at eliminating dead clusters and preserving codebook capacity.
1 million vectors, k = 16,384, 5 epochs, mean over 5 seeds; only the revival policy varies. A cluster counts as dead when fewer than ten vectors are assigned to it at the end, a thousandth of an average cluster. Imbalance: how uneven the cluster sizes are (1 = all equal). From the paper’s revival ablation table.
We validated e-means on 24 different embedding and synthetic datasets and configurations (see paper). For the video we ran 234 configurations of e-means against k-means (16 datasets, 100k to 100M points): explore every curve in the results map.
Repo: faiss/contrib/e_means.
If you use e-means, please cite the paper (arXiv:2611.09501):

articles.title: Crypto foundation demanded employees endorse suicide pledge
articles.body:
On a Friday in March, employees at an international technology foundation received a 38-page document outlining leadership’s vision for the foundation for the next 1,000 years.
The document went out to all employees of The Ethereum Foundation, a nonprofit organization registered in Switzerland that supports Ethereum, a popular cryptocurrency platform and the second-largest blockchain network in the world, valued at about $300 billion, according to a federal lawsuit filed by a Boulder resident Wednesday in U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado.
Titled “The Ethereum Foundation Mandate,” the document featured ethereal illustrated scenes of glowing lights and anime-style characters voyaging through dark forests. The pages featured white text against a navy blue background and were adorned with cartoon flowers, rainbows and diamonds.
And on page 11 — nestled between a winking anime woman and three yellow cats — was a suicide pledge.
Authors, maintainers, editors and distributors of “this software” would pledge to ensure the software remained free and publicly accessible, and would also vow to “take his or her own life with a sword upon failure to uphold any of the pledges in this license,” the illustration read. It was labeled “Source Seppuku License,” an apparent reference to a traditional Japanese ritual suicide.
When the document went out on that Friday in March, employees were told to commit to the principles in the mandate by Monday or quit their jobs, according to the lawsuit brought by Kayleen Fulton, a Boulder woman who was fired from the Ethereum Foundation after she led employee resistance to the suicide pledge.
Employees were to return a form with one of two options checked, according to a copy of the document included in legal filings.
Choice one: “I personally commit to the direction set out in the mandate, I commit to help translate it into thoroughly reasoned strategies for my domain, and I commit to an exclusive and energetic focus on the mission-critical tasks necessary for its implementation. From today and until my last day at the EF.”
Or choice two: “I cannot confidently commit to the above and would like to request my extra months of compensation and leave the EF without undue delay.”
An email to the foundation seeking comment on this story was not immediately returned Thursday, but a foundation leader at the time told employees the suicide pledge was not meant to be taken literally, according to the lawsuit. After employee pushback, managers updated the commitment form to clarify that the form had “nothing to do with literal seppuku,” according to the lawsuit.
Resistance to the suicide pledge was swift and vocal, and began when the Ethereum Foundation’s board put out a draft of the mandate to staff in late February, Fulton alleged in the lawsuit. Employees soon asked whether they were pledging to die by suicide and wondered in workplace forums whether the pledge was a test of their loyalty to Ethereum’s core principles. One employee referenced a colleague’s recent death by suicide.
“I have a new hire joining tomorrow,” another employee wrote in a discussion about the suicide pledge, according to the lawsuit. “The first thing he’s going to see… is a motion to drop a clause that mandates employees commit the ultimate sacrifice by falling on a sword.”
Nearly 80 of the foundation’s 250 or so employees voted to nix the suicide pledge after the draft was released, according to the lawsuit, but leadership at the Ethereum Foundation ignored their objections and included the pledge word-for-word in the final version of the mandate. The final published version presented the suicide pledge in an illustration instead of including it in the main body of the mandate, as it had been in the draft version.
The mandate’s visual aesthetic — the anime and other illustrations — reflected imagery from a controversial online figure who was known to promote “white nationalist ideology and disturbing pro-anorexia content,” according to the lawsuit.
When an Ethereum Foundation board member objected to the aesthetic, Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin responded that “the controversialness (sic) of those aesthetics is itself part of the point,” according to the lawsuit.
After demanding that employees agree to the mandate, Bastian Aue, co-executive director of the Ethereum Foundation, defended the suicide pledge to employees as “part of the artwork of the mandate.”
It was, he said, “a cultural reference like other elements in there. Chosen deliberately, but not meant to be taken literally.”
In the days after the mandate was pushed out to employees, Fulton and a colleague organized and sent the foundation’s board a letter in which 53 employees endorsed the mandate’s general direction but declined to return the commitment form. The employees also declined to resign, according to the lawsuit.
Aue ultimately allowed the letter-signers to keep their jobs. But he fired Fulton and her colleague who helped organize the letter. Buterin later told Fulton — who had just been diagnosed with cancer — that the firing was about company dynamics, according to the lawsuit.
“If you reward making a stink with outcomes, then everyone will know that essentially making that kind of show both internally and externally is the way to cause outcomes inside of the EF,” he said, according to the lawsuit, which cited a recorded conversation between the pair.
The mandate started an exodus at the Ethereum Foundation, according to the lawsuit. The board member who’d objected to the mandate’s visual aesthetics started a sabbatical the day Fulton was fired and resigned in June. By September, eight senior employees had left, according to the lawsuit, and most of the 53 people who signed the letter had resigned or been terminated.
Fulton, who had earned a salary of $195,000 in her role at the Ethereum Foundation, sued for disability discrimination, retaliation, interference with her rights under the Family and Medical Leave Act, unfair employment practices and related claims. Her lawsuit notes that the Ethereum Foundation “does not hire or pay its United States staff in its own name,” but instead uses employer-of-record service companies.
One of her attorneys, James Bartolomei, declined to comment Thursday, saying the lawsuit spoke for itself.
Get more Colorado news by signing up for our daily Your Morning Dozen email newsletter.

An email to the foundation seeking comment on this story was not immediately returned Thursday, but a foundation leader at the time told employees the suicide pledge was not meant to be taken literally, according to the lawsuit. After employee pushback, managers updated the commitment form to clarify that the form had “nothing to do with literal seppuku,” according to the lawsuit.
Resistance to the suicide pledge was swift and vocal, and began when the Ethereum Foundation’s board put out a draft of the mandate to staff in late February, Fulton alleged in the lawsuit. Employees soon asked whether they were pledging to die by suicide and wondered in workplace forums whether the pledge was a test of their loyalty to Ethereum’s core principles. One employee referenced a colleague’s recent death by suicide.
“I have a new hire joining tomorrow,” another employee wrote in a discussion about the suicide pledge, according to the lawsuit. “The first thing he’s going to see… is a motion to drop a clause that mandates employees commit the ultimate sacrifice by falling on a sword.”
Nearly 80 of the foundation’s 250 or so employees voted to nix the suicide pledge after the draft was released, according to the lawsuit, but leadership at the Ethereum Foundation ignored their objections and included the pledge word-for-word in the final version of the mandate. The final published version presented the suicide pledge in an illustration instead of including it in the main body of the mandate, as it had been in the draft version.
The mandate’s visual aesthetic — the anime and other illustrations — reflected imagery from a controversial online figure who was known to promote “white nationalist ideology and disturbing pro-anorexia content,” according to the lawsuit.
When an Ethereum Foundation board member objected to the aesthetic, Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin responded that “the controversialness (sic) of those aesthetics is itself part of the point,” according to the lawsuit.
After demanding that employees agree to the mandate, Bastian Aue, co-executive director of the Ethereum Foundation, defended the suicide pledge to employees as “part of the artwork of the mandate.”
It was, he said, “a cultural reference like other elements in there. Chosen deliberately, but not meant to be taken literally.”
In the days after the mandate was pushed out to employees, Fulton and a colleague organized and sent the foundation’s board a letter in which 53 employees endorsed the mandate’s general direction but declined to return the commitment form. The employees also declined to resign, according to the lawsuit.
Aue ultimately allowed the letter-signers to keep their jobs. But he fired Fulton and her colleague who helped organize the letter. Buterin later told Fulton — who had just been diagnosed with cancer — that the firing was about company dynamics, according to the lawsuit.
“If you reward making a stink with outcomes, then everyone will know that essentially making that kind of show both internally and externally is the way to cause outcomes inside of the EF,” he said, according to the lawsuit, which cited a recorded conversation between the pair.
The mandate started an exodus at the Ethereum Foundation, according to the lawsuit. The board member who’d objected to the mandate’s visual aesthetics started a sabbatical the day Fulton was fired and resigned in June. By September, eight senior employees had left, according to the lawsuit, and most of the 53 people who signed the letter had resigned or been terminated.
Fulton, who had earned a salary of $195,000 in her role at the Ethereum Foundation, sued for disability discrimination, retaliation, interference with her rights under the Family and Medical Leave Act, unfair employment practices and related claims. Her lawsuit notes that the Ethereum Foundation “does not hire or pay its United States staff in its own name,” but instead uses employer-of-record service companies.
One of her attorneys, James Bartolomei, declined to comment Thursday, saying the lawsuit spoke for itself.
Get more Colorado news by signing up for our daily Your Morning Dozen email newsletter.

articles.title: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
articles.body:
Computer Science > Computation and Language
  [Submitted on 9 Oct 2026]
Title:Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running $21\times$ faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running $10\times$ faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being $31\times$ faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations.
